# English

## Billed by contacts, sold as an operating system

URL: https://upahje.my/en/articles/kuasaos-crm-with-a-costume
Checked: 2026-11-26

KuasaOS launched in October 2026 as "Malaysia's First AI Agents-Powered Business OS", with three agents given names — ARA, HIRA and SAFA — and a launch offer of fifty million free AI credits to the first thousand businesses. It is a real product from a real company, FunnelEvo Sdn Bhd, and it ships weekly.

Our view, stated once: it is a CRM with a costume on.

The evidence is not a leak or an insider. It is on the vendor's own pages, read on 26 November 2026.

## The meter tells you what a product is

Look at how something is priced and you learn what it thinks it is selling. Kuasa's plans:

| Plan | Price | Contacts | Notable |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Free | RM0 | 250 | lifetime trial |
| Starter | RM49/month, billed yearly | 1,500 | automations, WhatsApp API, remove branding |
| Professional | RM199/month, billed yearly | 4,500 | 3 chatbots, 15 order forms, AI landing pages |
| Business | RM499/month, billed yearly | 10,000 | 5 chatbots, 35 order forms |

Every tier is metered by **contact count**. Not by agents run, not by documents processed, not by invoices issued, not by payslips calculated. Contacts. That is the meter a contact database uses, because contacts are the thing a contact database has.

An operating system would meter work: payroll runs, invoices filed, returns submitted, reconciliations closed. This one meters a list.

## The product's own words disagree with the launch's words

The pricing page footer, written by the company, reads:

> "The easy and effective CRM for closing deals"

The launch page, written by the same company in the same quarter, reads:

> "Say hello to your AI-powered business operating system."

One of those sentences is a description and the other is a category claim. A CRM for closing deals is a perfectly good product. Calling it an operating system is a positioning decision, and positioning is free — which is why it is the first thing every launch changes.

## What the feature list actually contains

We read the full comparison table. Counting mentions of the things a Malaysian business must do to stay out of trouble:

| Term | Mentions on the pricing page |
| --- | --- |
| payroll | 0 |
| PCB | 0 |
| EPF | 0 |
| SOCSO | 0 |
| SST | 0 |
| e-Invoice | 0 |
| accounting | 0 |
| HR | 0 |
| employee | 0 |

What is there: contacts, AI scoring, chatbots, order forms, AI landing pages, team members, custom fields, broadcasts, automations, WhatsApp API access.

None of that is worthless. All of it is a sales and marketing stack. A business in Malaysia does not get through a month on a sales stack, because the month also contains a payroll run, an SST return if it is registered, and — since 2024 — e-Invoice obligations that arrive whether or not your lead pipeline is full.

## The launch was an offer, not a capability

The October launch led with **fifty million AI credits for the first thousand businesses**, **up to 50% off**, and a hero section carrying four counters: total registrations, records under management, countries, years in business. On 26 November 2026, all four read **0**. That may be a rendering fault rather than a fact, but it is the version of the page the vendor is serving.

"Malaysia's first" is not a claim that can be checked, only asserted, and there are now at least three unrelated products using the Kuasa name — kuasa.ai, kuasa.io, and an open-source project called OpenKuasa which explicitly states in its README that it is unaffiliated with any company. When a category needs a disclaimer, the category is still being defined.

## What the agents are, as far as the evidence shows

ARA, HIRA and SAFA are presented as named employees. Naming is a good interface decision — a name is easier to talk about than a feature flag. It is not a capability.

The changelog for week three of November lists fixes and improvements across contacts, pipeline, forms, broadcasts and automations, plus Telegram receipt submission. That is the footprint of an assistant layered on a CRM: it reads what the CRM already stored and helps you act on it. Useful. Not an operating system, which would have to hold the ledger of the business rather than its conversations.

## What RM499 a month buys elsewhere

For the price of the top tier — RM5,988 a year — a Malaysian SME can buy a payroll service that calculates PCB correctly against the current schedule, or the accounting package that produces the SST-02 the return actually needs, or a year of both hosted tools and a freelancer to set them up.

That comparison is the whole argument. KuasaOS is not expensive in absolute terms; RM499 is a normal software bill. It is expensive **for a contact database**, and the pricing page gives no reason to think it is anything else.

## What would change our mind

Three things, all specific and all checkable:

1. A payroll run — EPF, SOCSO, EIS, PCB — calculated from the official tables, with the payslip produced.
2. An SST-02 summary, or an e-Invoice submission that goes through MyInvois and comes back with a validation link.
3. A pricing meter that charges per document or per run rather than per contact.

Ship any one of those and the phrase "business operating system" stops being decoration. Until then, the meter is the most honest sentence on the site.

## The claim

**A Malaysian business OS will be decided by PCB, SST-02 and e-Invoice, not by how well an agent is named — and at RM499 a month for a contact database, KuasaOS is selling the costume while the compliance work stays unbuilt. The first local product that files a return correctly will make every persona-named agent on the market look like what it is: a chat window with a business card.**

That is a wager, not a prophecy, and we will publish the correction the day a vendor proves it wrong.

## RM1.25 or 15%: what your own checkout costs

URL: https://upahje.my/en/articles/own-checkout-vs-commission
Checked: 2026-11-26

Two shops sell the same RM30 plate. One takes the order on its own site and pays **RM1.25** to collect the money. The other takes the order through a delivery platform that takes **15% to 25%** of the bill — between RM4.50 and RM7.50.

That gap is the whole argument for owning your own shop, and it is the reason the argument is more complicated than it sounds. Because the platform is not only charging you for payments. It is charging you for customers.

## The two rates, from the pages that print them

Payment gateways publish their prices. We read Billplz's pricing page on 26 November 2026:

| Item | Basic (free plan) | Standard (MYR 999/year) | Settlement |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Online banking (FPX), B2C | RM1.25 per transaction | RM0.75 per transaction | next business day |
| Online banking, B2B | RM3.00 | RM2.00 | next business day |
| Card, MYR | 1.8% | 1.5% | T+2 business days |
| Card, non-MYR | 3.8% | 3.5% | T+2 business days |
| Auto-deduct, MYR | 2.3% + RM1.25 | 2.0% + RM0.75 | T+2 business days |

Delivery platforms do not publish merchant commission. Grab and foodpanda have no public rate card for merchants, which is why the numbers in this article come from a regulator rather than a vendor: the Malaysia Competition Commission's decision on foodpanda, dated 11 September 2023, records commission bands in its Table 3 of **1–5%, 10–25%, 15–20% and 15–25%** depending on the service.

Those are recorded ranges from three years ago, not today's quoted rate. Any specific figure for your shop has to come from the contract someone puts in front of you — and that, on its own, tells you something about the two markets.

## The same order, costed twice

One RM30 order, no delivery:

| | Own checkout | Platform at 15% | Platform at 25% |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Customer pays | RM30.00 | RM30.00 | RM30.00 |
| Payment or commission | RM1.25 (FPX) | RM4.50 | RM7.50 |
| You keep | RM28.75 | RM25.50 | RM22.50 |
| Cost as a share | 4.2% | 15% | 25% |

At 15%, the platform costs **3.6 times** what an FPX payment costs. At 25%, **six times**. Over a hundred orders a month that is the difference between RM2,875 and RM2,250 kept — RM625 a month, RM7,500 a year, on a shop doing RM3,000 of revenue a month.

Now the same order delivered, because this is where the comparison usually gets dishonest. A platform's commission covers a rider. Your own checkout does not:

| | Own checkout + courier | Platform at 20% |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Customer pays | RM30.00 | RM30.00 |
| Payment | RM1.25 | included |
| Rider or courier | RM5.00–8.00, yours to arrange | included |
| You keep | RM20.75–23.75 | RM24.00 |

**At delivery, the platform is competitive.** That is the finding most "own your shop" articles skip, and it is the reason the honest answer to "should I leave the platform" is: not for delivery, probably yes for pickup and repeat customers.

![Three panels: a listing on someone else's site, an aggregator with riders, and your own storefront. Only the third keeps the customer list, and the third is the one where discovery becomes your job](/figures/own-shop-three-ways.svg)

## What a working independent shop looks like

mejamakan is a lauk delivery business in KL and Selangor that runs its own site instead of a platform page. What is publicly observable on 26 November 2026:

- A curated **weekly menu**, dishes grouped by day, tagged protein and vegetables, with rice as an add-on
- **Accounts and ordering on their own domain**, not a redirect to a marketplace
- **"From RM18/meal"** shown before checkout
- **Delivery Monday to Friday**, and a plan you **renew** — a subscription, not a one-off order
- **"3,000+ families served"**, their own figure, quoted as theirs
- Instagram as the front door: 16K followers, which is where the traffic comes from

![mejamakan.my captured at mobile width on 26 November 2026: a weekly menu grouped by day, each dish tagged protein or vegetables, with rice offered as an add-on](/figures/screens/mejamakan-menu.webp)

That last point is the part nobody puts in the pitch deck. The website is the checkout. The audience is the business.

We built the cheaper version of the same thing ourselves, and wrote it up separately: [One person, one kitchen](https://upahje.my/en/articles/we-built-our-own-storefront). husnieats is a one-person kitchen site with three dishes — Buttermilk Chicken RM12.90, Korean Chicken RM13.90, Teh O RM3.50 — and its payment flow is **a DuitNow QR code and a WhatsApp receipt**. No gateway, no commission, no platform: the fee is zero and the cost is a human checking the transfer before the kitchen starts. At three dishes and a handful of orders a day, that trade is correct. At fifty orders a day it stops being correct, because the human becomes the bottleneck.

## The arithmetic that decides it

Write down four numbers:

1. **Orders a month.** Ours: whatever your till says.
2. **Average bill.** Higher bills make percentage commission hurt more; lower bills make per-transaction fees hurt more.
3. **Commission rate** from your actual contract, not a blog.
4. **Your payment cost** — RM1.25 an order on FPX, or 1.8% on cards.

Break-even orders a month, ignoring delivery:

> commission rate × average bill × orders = RM1.25 × orders + the cost of getting those customers yourself

The left side is what the platform takes. The right side is what your own checkout costs **plus the marketing you now have to do**. That marketing term is the one everybody leaves out, and it is the reason a shop with no audience should stay on the platform until it has one.

## What we would tell a shop with three dishes

Stay on the platform for delivery, because the rider is the expensive part and they buy it in bulk. Put your own checkout in front of the customers who already know you — the ones who order every week, who message you directly, who would rather pay RM1.25 of fees than see you lose RM7.50 of margin.

Then watch one number: **how many of your orders arrive through a channel you own**. When that share passes half, the platform is a delivery contractor rather than a shopfront, and the commission conversation changes completely.

## A 9-ending works on new items. Nobody has proved the rest.

URL: https://upahje.my/en/articles/price-endings-nine
Checked: 2026-11-26

A 9 at the end of a price tag is the most common pricing move in Malaysian retail and the least tested one. The best evidence is three American field experiments published in 2003: the $9 ending "increased demand in all three experiments", the lift was strongest on items the retailer had not sold before, and the authors note it weakens once a sale sticker is already doing the work. No effect size is published. No Malaysian experiment exists. So the honest reading is narrow — it can move a new item, and nobody knows by how much.

## What the three experiments found

The paper is Anderson and Simester, *Effects of $9 Price Endings on Retail Sales: Evidence from Field Experiments*, in Quantitative Marketing and Economics volume 1, pages 93 to 110. The design matters more than the conclusion: price endings were manipulated in real stores, not in a lab, and the authors report two conclusions from the data.

First, the $9 ending raised demand in all three experiments. Second, the increase was stronger for new items than for items the retailer had sold in previous years.

## The effect is conditional, and the authors say so

A third sentence in the abstract is the useful one for a shop: "There is also some evidence that $9 price endings are less effective when retailers use 'Sale' cues." The hedge is the authors' own.

That reading fits how a price tag works. If a red sticker already tells the customer the price is low, a 9 at the end is a second signal saying the same thing, and two signals do not double the effect. The authors offer an explanation rather than a proof: 9-endings "may be more effective when customers have limited information, which may in turn help to explain why retailers do not use $9 price endings on every item."

## No percentage appears in this article

The abstract publishes no effect size, and the full text is paywalled, so the "24% more sales" figure that circulates with this paper's name cannot be checked here and is not printed. A directional finding is what the evidence supports: endings moved demand, with the conditions above.

Those are the honest limits of a two-decade-old American result, and a Malaysian price decision made on it is an extrapolation.

## Malaysia has the convention and not the data

RM2.90 and RM19.90 are everywhere in Malaysian retail, which shows the convention, not its effect. No Malaysian field experiment on price endings surfaced in our search, and no regulator publishes a retail price-ending study.

| What is published | Value | Where |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Field experiments in the paper | 3 | abstract |
| Publication year and volume | 2003, volume 1 | journal record |
| Countries covered | 1, the United States | abstract |
| Effect size published | none | abstract |
| Malaysian field experiments found | 0 | absence check |
| Conditions the authors name | 2, new versus established, and sale cues | abstract |

The zero in that table is the row a Malaysian owner should read twice. It is an absence, not a finding that 9-endings fail here.

## What a shop can do with this

1. Test the 9 on a new item, where the published effect was strongest.
2. Do not stack a 9-ending on top of a sale sticker.
3. Run the test for two weeks on comparable volume, and compare units, not revenue.
4. Keep the old price visible in the same test, because a price change and a price-ending change are two different experiments.
5. Do not treat a 9 as a substitute for a price the customer can justify.

For a small Malaysian shop, the 9 is a test, not a policy. The evidence says it can move demand on something new; it does not say by how much, and it does not say anything about your customers. Spend a fortnight finding out rather than a year assuming.

## Twelve jobs a rented GPU finishes, and three it cannot

URL: https://upahje.my/en/articles/rented-gpu-jobs-malaysia
Checked: 2026-11-26

A rented GPU is a tool with one shape: it is excellent at work that starts, finishes, and stops. Everything in this article is sorted by that. If a job has a beginning and an end, renting a card for it is now cheap enough to be unremarkable. If a job has to be awake at three in the morning, renting is usually the wrong answer and an API is usually the right one.

The rate, read from Vast.ai today: an RTX 5060 Ti with 16 GB of VRAM starts at USD 0.09 an hour with a median of USD 0.13, which is about 55 sen an hour at the rate we publish at. An H100 SXM is USD 1.73, about RM7.12. Every cost in this article is that rate multiplied by your time — a formula, not a quote, because your dataset is not ours.

## The memory ladder, which decides what you can attempt

VRAM, not price, is what rules jobs out. For models in four-bit precision, the working rule is roughly 0.6 GB per billion parameters, plus room for the context you feed in.

| VRAM | What it unlocks | Representative card | Rate from |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 8 GB | Small classifiers, OCR, transcription, embedding a document set | RTX 5060 | USD 0.09/hr |
| 16 GB | 7B models at 4-bit, LoRA fine-tunes of small models, image generation | RTX 5060 Ti | USD 0.09/hr |
| 24 GB | 13B at 4-bit, larger fine-tunes, video work | RTX 4090 / 3090 | USD 0.07–0.09/hr |
| 48 GB | 34B at 4-bit, multi-GPU-free training runs | RTX 6000 class | quote by host |
| 80 GB | 70B at 4-bit, full fine-tunes of small models | H100 | USD 1.73/hr |

The jump from 16 GB to 80 GB costs nineteen times more per hour. Almost nothing a Malaysian SME needs sits on the far side of that jump.

## The twelve jobs

Each row is a job we would rent a card for. Time is a realistic band, not a benchmark, and the cost column is the median 16 GB rate applied to that band.

| # | Job | Time | Cost at USD 0.13/hr |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Train a small classifier or regressor on your own rows | minutes | under USD 0.05 |
| 2 | Fine-tune a small language model on your own text (LoRA) | 1–4 hours | USD 0.13–0.52 |
| 3 | Build embeddings for a document set, for search or answers | 10–60 min | USD 0.02–0.13 |
| 4 | Transcribe a year of call recordings or voice notes | 1–6 hours | USD 0.13–0.78 |
| 5 | Extract fields from invoices, receipts, delivery orders at volume | 30–120 min | USD 0.07–0.26 |
| 6 | Generate or clean product photography at catalogue scale | 1–3 hours | USD 0.13–0.39 |
| 7 | Caption and subtitle video, including Malay | 2–8 hours | USD 0.26–1.04 |
| 8 | Deduplicate and normalise a messy customer or product table | 10–40 min | USD 0.02–0.09 |
| 9 | Synthetic data to test a rule or an assistant before launch | 1–2 hours | USD 0.13–0.26 |
| 10 | Evaluate two models against your own examples | 30–90 min | USD 0.07–0.20 |
| 11 | Render a Blender or CAD animation across many frames | 2–12 hours | USD 0.26–1.56 |
| 12 | Batch-process images: resize, background removal, watermark | 20–60 min | USD 0.04–0.13 |

Read the right-hand column twice. Twelve jobs, and the most expensive one in the table is under two ringgit. The reason to think about this at all is not the money — it is that a card you forget to switch off bills 24 hours a day, and a card left running for a month costs USD 94, which is more than a year of the API you were avoiding.

### 1. Train something small

The cheapest job on the list and the one most often overcomplicated. If your data fits in a spreadsheet, the model is minutes, not hours. We trained a 1,607-row filter in **five seconds** for four cents.

Worth renting when: the dataset is yours, the question is narrow, and the answer needs to be reproducible next year.

### 2. Fine-tune a small language model

Four-bit quantisation is what made this ordinary: a 7B model needs about 5 GB at four bits, so a 16 GB card can fine-tune a small model with room left for the optimiser state. The output is an adapter measured in tens of megabytes — ours was 73 MB.

What it is for: a model that writes in your voice, classifies your categories, or answers from your documents. What it is not for: teaching a model facts it never saw. Fine-tuning changes how a model talks and what it prefers; it does not reliably install a price list.

### 3. Embeddings for search

Point a card at a folder of PDFs, contracts, product sheets or past quotes and produce vectors you can search. This is the cheapest useful AI job there is, and it runs in minutes on a 16 GB card. The output is small, permanent and yours.

### 4. Transcription

Whisper-class models transcribe reliably and handle Malay better than the free tiers of most products, and the job is embarrassingly parallel: split the audio, run the pieces, join the transcripts. A year of recordings is an afternoon.

This is the job we would recommend first to almost any SME, because the input already exists — call recordings, voice notes, meeting audio — and the output is searchable text you can act on.

### 5. Invoice and document extraction

Malaysian businesses now generate structured e-Invoice data, but the incoming side is still PDFs, photographs of delivery orders, and supplier invoices in three languages. Extracting fields at volume is a batch job, it needs no large model, and it pays for itself the first month you stop typing.

### 6 and 12. Images

Product photography at catalogue scale, and bulk processing — resizing, background removal, watermarking. Both are batch, both fit on a 16 GB card, both are cheaper rented by the hour than subscribed by the month if the work is periodic rather than constant.

### 7. Video

Captioning and subtitling, including Malay, is the highest-value video job because it is the one that makes video searchable and accessible. It is also slow — hours, not minutes — which makes the hourly rate matter more here than anywhere else in the table.

### 8 to 10. The unglamorous ones that pay

Deduplicating a customer table, generating synthetic examples to test an assistant, and evaluating two models against your own cases. None of these produce anything a customer sees, and all three are why a launch does not embarrass you. They are also the jobs most often skipped, because they feel like overhead until the first wrong answer reaches a customer.

### 11. Rendering

Blender and CAD work is the classic GPU rental: frames are independent, the job is finite, and a card you rent for six hours beats a workstation you buy for six thousand ringgit if you render twice a year.

## The three it cannot do

1. **Stay awake.** A marketplace instance can be reclaimed. Anything that must answer at three in the morning needs a host that promises to be there, and that is a different product with a different bill.
2. **Be trusted with residency.** Nothing on a marketplace tells you which country the machine sits in. For customer data under Malaysian expectations, that is a decision, not a detail.
3. **Replace an API for small volume.** One image a day, a hundred chat messages a week, a single transcription a month: the API is cheaper, because you are paying for a card that idles between jobs.

## How to price your own job

Take the hourly rate, multiply by the hours you expect, then multiply by three. The first factor is published, the second is a guess, and the third is the correction everyone learns the hard way: dataset preparation, failed runs and the time you spend reading logs all bill as instance hours if you leave the machine on.

Two habits cut that multiplier:

- Write results after every unit of work, so a crash costs the last unit rather than the whole run.
- End the script with a shutdown command, so a finished job cannot keep billing.

## What we would do first, in Malaysia

1. **Transcribe your voice notes and calls.** Existing data, immediate value, an afternoon of compute.
2. **Extract fields from incoming invoices.** The pain is weekly and the job is batch.
3. **Embed your documents so search works.** Small, permanent, and it makes every later assistant better.

The order matters less than the first step: rent the card for a job with an end, switch it off, and look at the bill. It will be smaller than the caution that stopped you, and the second job will be easier than the first.

## USD 0.04 of GPU time, and the dataset was the work

URL: https://upahje.my/en/articles/rented-gpu-what-it-finishes
Checked: 2026-11-26

The bill for the whole run was four cents. Twelve minutes on a rented RTX 5060 Ti at USD 0.1981 an hour, of which the model trained for five seconds and the dataset took fourteen to build. The rest of the twelve minutes was a machine being rented while a person read logs.

That ratio is the point of this article. Almost everything written about renting a GPU is about the hourly rate, and the hourly rate is the least interesting number in the decision. What matters is how many minutes of billed time a finished job costs you, and for most small work that number is embarrassing in the other direction: the compute is cheap enough that the expensive part is being ready to use it.

## The hourly rate is the wrong unit

The same card, priced on Vast.ai today: an RTX 5060 Ti with 16 GB of VRAM lists from USD 0.09 an hour, with a median of USD 0.13. The instance in this article was rented in June 2026 at USD 0.1981 an hour, so the platform price has roughly halved in five months.

| Card | VRAM | Price from | Median | Source, read |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| RTX 5060 Ti | 16 GB | USD 0.09/hr | USD 0.13/hr | Vast.ai pricing, 26 Nov 2026 |
| RTX 4090 | 24 GB | USD 0.07/hr | USD 0.47/hr | same |
| RTX 5090 | 32 GB | USD 0.39/hr | USD 0.67/hr | same |
| H100 SXM | 80 GB | USD 1.73/hr | USD 1.73/hr | same |

Two things in that table are worth reading twice. The floor and the median can be far apart, because a marketplace is a set of individual hosts with their own prices and their own reliability. And the H100, the card everyone reasons about, costs nineteen times the floor price of the card that did this job.

A twelve-minute job at today's floor is under two cents. A twelve-minute job on an H100 is thirty-five. Neither is a business expense; both are smaller than the coffee you drink while waiting.

## Job one: train something small enough to finish

The job was a filter, not a model that trades. A set of nine strategies had already generated 1,607 historical trade entries across currency pairs, and the question was whether a model could tell a winning entry from a losing one using only what was knowable at entry: the signal's strength, volatility, recent returns, the day of the week, the month, and which instrument and strategy fired.

Sixteen features per trade. Identity as embeddings, so the model learns symbol and strategy behaviour instead of being told. A two-layer network, 64 wide, no attention, no pretraining, no billion parameters.

Trained on the card in five seconds. Cross-validated five ways, out-of-sample AUC 0.6021 — per fold 0.53, 0.66, 0.63, 0.60, 0.53. Not a good model in absolute terms. Good enough to act as a filter, which is what it was asked to be:

| Filter threshold | Trades kept | Win rate | Mean return | Sharpe per trade | Annualised |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| none | 1,607 | 44.8% | +1.29% | 0.167 | +2.64 |
| 0.40 | 1,081 | 50.4% | +2.12% | 0.271 | +3.51 |
| 0.55 | 310 | 54.5% | +3.91% | 0.362 | +2.52 |
| 0.60 | 137 | 55.5% | +4.46% | 0.369 | +1.70 |

At 0.40 the filter drops a third of the trades and the annualised figure rises from 2.64 to 3.51. At 0.60 the per-trade numbers look best and the annualised figure collapses, because there is nothing left to trade. That shape is the whole argument against optimising for accuracy: a filter that is right more often can still make less money.

And the first model tried was a transformer, which overfitted immediately on 1,607 rows. The architecture was chosen by the size of the dataset, not by what was fashionable. Five seconds of compute is not the constraint here — 1,607 examples is.

## Job two: sweep, and know when to stop

The second job is the one that eats money: trying configurations. A sweep script scoped **324** combinations — model width, depth, sequence length, forecast horizon, seeds — over ten chronological folds, up to 200 epochs each, effective batch 512 through 256 with gradient accumulation, mixed precision to fit a small card.

Twenty-two finished. The instance was destroyed deliberately to stop paying for storage, and that decision is the part worth copying. The results were not nothing:

| Setting | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Best width and depth | d_model 32, 2 layers |
| Best sequence length | 12 bars |
| Best forecast horizon | 12 bars |
| Validation accuracy | 0.7432 |
| Test accuracy | 0.7495 |
| Test AUC | 0.8212 |

Three findings came out of 22 runs rather than 324. Small models won: `d_model` above 64 added overfit risk, not signal. A twelve-hour horizon beat twenty-four and forty-eight, because the further out you predict the more noise you are asking the model to memorise. And the result was stable across seeds — the same configuration with seeds 42, 123 and 7777 gave AUCs between 0.814 and 0.821, which is what tells you the number is a property of the data rather than of one lucky initialisation.

The infrastructure that made stopping safe is unglamorous and worth a paragraph. The driver script set up the environment, pulled the code, logged `nvidia-smi` every sixty seconds, wrote results after every completed configuration so a crash resumed rather than restarted, and ended by shutting the instance down itself. A full sweep was scoped at about two days; the quick three-configuration check at about two hours. The stop command is what turns a two-day plan into a two-hour decision.

## Job three: fine-tune on your own text

The third job is the one a small business actually has. Not training from scratch — teaching a small model your own words. A four-bit quantised 1.5-billion-parameter model, fine-tuned with QLoRA on trade annotations, produced a 73 MB adapter file. That is the entire deliverable: not a model, a 73 MB delta that sits on top of a base model you did not pay to train.

The economics are why this is now ordinary. Quantising the base model to four bits, which is what QLoRA does, is what makes a 1.5B model fit alongside its own gradients on a consumer card. The method is published and the tooling is free.

For a Malaysian SME the equivalent job is a classifier or a writer over your own material: WhatsApp replies, product descriptions, e-Invoice line items, supplier emails. Static data, small volume, one card, an afternoon.

## Job four: hosting, which is where this breaks

The first three jobs are batch work: start the box, run, stop it, pay for minutes. Hosting is the opposite and it is where a rented GPU is the wrong tool.

- **Interruption.** Marketplace instances can be reclaimed. A price-sensitive instance is a bet on staying up.
- **Storage.** Data sitting on a rented disk bills by the hour whether or not anything computes. That is exactly the reason the sweep above stopped at 22 configurations.
- **State.** A hosted assistant needs the model resident, which means a card idle most of the day at the hourly rate.
- **Residency.** Nothing in this arrangement tells you which country the machine is in, and for customer data that is not a footnote.

If the requirement is a model that answers at three in the morning, an API priced per million tokens is almost always cheaper than a card priced per hour. Renting a GPU wins when the work is finished and the instance is off.

## The bill

| Run | Billed time | Cost |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Trade filter, 1,607 rows, 5-fold | ~12 min at USD 0.1981/hr | USD 0.04 |
| Sweep, 22 of 324 configurations | instance hours, plus storage | not itemised here |
| LoRA adapter, 73 MB | one session | not itemised here |

Four cents is about sixteen sen at the rate we publish at, 4.1155 ringgit to the dollar on 24 November 2026. It is not the cost of training a trading model. It is the cost of one experiment against a dataset that already existed, on a card rented by the minute, and the honest version of the claim is the narrow one.

## What to do first

1. Pick a job that finishes in minutes, not hours. Classification, extraction, a small regression, a fine-tune over a thousand rows.
2. Build the dataset before you rent anything. In our run it took three times as long as the training.
3. Cap the budget, not the ambition: an hourly card plus a self-destruct command is a smaller commitment than a subscription.
4. Write results to disk after every unit of work, so an interrupted instance costs you the last unit rather than all of it.
5. Keep the dataset. It is the only asset here that does not bill by the hour.

## Your simulated customer says yes. Real ones leave.

URL: https://upahje.my/en/articles/simulated-customer-says-yes
Checked: 2026-11-26

Two studies published this year tested whether a language model can stand in for a customer. Both used real data. They reached opposite conclusions, and the difference between them is the whole article: the simulation is accurate about the average basket and dishonest about the person who walks out.

If you are being sold "AI market research" — or thinking of using it to test a price, a shelf, a brand deal or a sales script — the split matters more than any single accuracy figure.

## One: the simulation that matched the household's own history

The first study built shoppers out of household purchase records, gave them a store directory and photographs of shelves, and asked them to plan a trip and pick products. Then it compared their baskets against six public datasets from three countries.

The headline result is not "the model is good at shopping". It is that **the synthetic baskets predicted held-out purchases as well as the households' own past trips did**. A model that only reads text has no access to the store, the shelf or the label; add vision and it gets close to the best available predictor of what a household buys next, which is that household's own history.

Three more findings from that paper:

- **Group differences** produced by synthetic shoppers correlated with real ones **twice as strongly** as a trained regression did.
- Without fitting anything, the simulators reproduced **alcohol purchases by gender and age in Russia**, and **trip size by store distance in Taiwan**.
- At the level of a **single shelf choice**, the model confounded the product with **its position on the shelf and its letter label** — which is why the authors built a dataset of shelf renderings that vary product, position, label, viewpoint and price independently.

That last point is the useful warning for anyone designing packaging or shelf layout: the model's answer about your product may be an answer about where you put it.

## Two: the simulation that cannot walk away

The second study is harder to sell and more useful. It ignored surveys and used **2,790 real sales conversations**, **793 of them with verified payment outcomes** — actual money, actual yes and no.

They measured whether a simulator, playing the customer, reproduces the *decision dynamics* of the real person. It does, for buyers. For non-buyers it does not:

| Measure | Real non-buyers | Simulated non-buyers |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Pull toward the purchase frame | reference | **+0.40** (d = 0.38, p < 0.001) |
| Expressing resistance | 25.1% | **13.5%** |
| Continuing to deliberate instead | 21.9% | **40.1%** |

Buyers were reproduced almost exactly (bias +0.09). Non-buyers were pulled toward buying, their stated resistance roughly halved, and their hesitation converted into more questions about price rather than an exit. No simulated customer fabricated a purchase — the failure is subtler than lying. It is that they **do not leave**.

The authors name it the **disengagement deficit**, and then do the thing that makes the paper credible: they try to fix it. Telling the simulator explicitly that it may disengage cuts the marginal bias fivefold, but barely moves the outcome-conditioned contrast (d = 0.34, p = 0.008). The bias is not in the instructions you give the simulator; it is in the situation you put it in. It also replicates across model families (DeepSeek: d = 0.41, p = 0.002).

Their closing sentence is the one to remember: **real non-buyers say "not now" and stop; simulated non-buyers ask about price.**

## How accurate is accurate

The number usually quoted comes from a third project, Twin-2K-500: digital twins built for **2,058 US participants**, answering the same survey questions their real counterparts answered. Across **17 tasks the twins' predictions were 71.72% accurate**, and the paper is careful to compare that against how much a person's own answers change when asked twice.

That comparison is the honest frame for all of this. An accuracy figure means nothing until you know the **test-retest ceiling** — how much the real human varies against themselves. A simulator that matches a person 72% of the time sounds impressive; if that person only matches themselves 75% of the time, the simulator is nearly at the ceiling. If the ceiling is 95%, there is a large gap.

Earlier work in this line — conditioning a model on a real person's survey backstory to reproduce their answers — found the same shape: **aggregate distributions reproduce well, individuals less so**. Two years of results now point the same way.

## Where you can actually apply it

The split above gives a clean rule. **Use simulation where the question is about a population and the answer is a distribution. Distrust it where the question is about a decision and the answer is a rate.**

| Use | What you simulate | Evidence strength |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Shelf and pack tests** | Your product against competitors on a rendered shelf, at different facings, positions and prices | Strong — this is exactly what the first study validated, with the position/label confound noted |
| **Price perception** | Whether a price reads as cheap or premium next to named alternatives | Moderate — display and price responses were within measured ranges, not exact |
| **Brand image** | Descriptions of how a brand is perceived, before and after a change of logo, colour or copy | Moderate — aggregate survey fidelity is the best-supported claim in this line of work |
| **Brand deals** | How a partnership or sponsorship announcement reads to a segment; which objections surface first | Weak but useful — generates the objection list, does not measure approval |
| **Sales scripts** | Which objection a script invites, and which phrasing reduces friction | Weak on rates, useful on variety — the simulator will overstate progress |
| **Conversion estimates** | "How many of 100 would buy" | **Don't.** This is precisely the quantity the disengagement deficit corrupts |

### Running a brand-deal simulation honestly

1. Write the deal down the way a customer would encounter it — a post, a shelf talker, a press line — not the way a deck describes it.
2. Give each simulated respondent a **backstory from your own customers**, not a demographic stereotype. The strongest results in this literature come from conditioning on real records.
3. Ask open questions and count the **objections**, not the approvals.
4. Run the same prompt against **two model families**. If the objection list does not survive that, it was a prompt artefact.
5. Take the top three objections to **ten real customers** before you decide anything.

Step five is the whole method. The simulation is a hypothesis generator with a good hit rate on distributions; the ten conversations are the measurement.

### For brand image specifically

Simulation is at its best when you have **a corpus of real things people said** and you want to know how a change lands. Feed the model your reviews, your DMs, your complaint emails — then ask what the same population would say about the new logo, the new price, the new packaging. What you get is a plausible distribution of reactions, not a measurement of them.

What it cannot tell you is whether the brand will be *talked about*, because that depends on reach, novelty and timing, none of which live in the model.

## The Malaysian caveat

None of these studies used Malaysian shoppers, and none used Bahasa Melayu. The mechanisms are general; the numbers are not. Treat every figure in this article as evidence about the method, not as a parameter for your shop.

Two specific risks here: shelf conventions differ (a top-shelf position is not universal), and a model's Malay is drawn from a different mix of text than your customers' Malay. A simulation in Malay should be treated as a rougher instrument than the same simulation in English, and the papers give no figure for how much rougher.

## The rule, in one line

Simulate the **population**, measure the **decision**. A synthetic customer is a good way to find out what people might say and a bad way to find out how many will pay — and the papers above are the receipt for both halves of that sentence.

## One person, one kitchen: we built the storefront and ran it

URL: https://upahje.my/en/articles/we-built-our-own-storefront
Checked: 2026-11-26

This is not an argument against delivery platforms. It is a demonstration of what a single person can now do without one.

We had been writing about the cost of owning your own shop — commission rates, payment fees, the discovery problem — and the writing was starting to feel like advice we had not tested. So we built the thing instead. **husnieats** is a working storefront for one kitchen: three dishes, cooked to order, pickup in Section 7 or delivered by a runner, taking real orders through a site that runs on our own infrastructure.

husnieats is ours; nothing else in this article is.

## What it actually does

Not a menu page with a WhatsApp link. A storefront with the three systems any shop needs to take money without a platform:

**1. Order taking.** The menu is three dishes — Buttermilk Chicken at RM12.90, Korean Chicken at RM13.90, Teh O at RM3.50 — each with a description and an Add button. The customer chooses pickup or delivery, and the delivery price appears **before** they commit, not after.

![The husnieats ordering flow: pick your food, pay by DuitNow, send the receipt on WhatsApp — three steps, no platform in between](/figures/screens/husnieats-ordering.webp)

**2. Ticketing.** Every order gets a short, speakable ticket — A001 through A999, then B001 — because the kitchen board and the runner's phone both need a handle a human can shout across a room. The customer's link uses a separate random token instead, because sequential numbers are guessable and a public URL must not be.

**3. Payment reconciliation.** The customer scans a DuitNow QR, pays the exact amount the order shows, and sends the receipt on WhatsApp. A human checks it, then the kitchen starts. That is the whole payment stack: one QR code, one message, one pair of eyes.

Orders and deliveries are tracked as two separate states, because a pickup order has no rider to wait for. And the money is stored as integer sen, rounded to the nearest ten — the smallest amount that appears on a Malaysian bill — rather than as a decimal that drifts.

![The husnieats menu at mobile width: three dishes, prices, add buttons. One kitchen, three dishes, because that is what can be cooked properly to order](/figures/screens/husnieats-menu.webp)

## The fraction

Here is what that replaces. A payment gateway charges **RM1.25** to collect RM30 by FPX on its free plan, or RM0.75 on a RM999-a-year plan. A card costs **1.8%**. Those are published prices, read from Billplz's page on 26 November 2026.

A delivery platform takes commission. Neither Grab nor foodpanda publishes a merchant rate card, so the only recorded numbers are the bands in the Competition Commission's foodpanda decision of 11 September 2023: **1–5%, 10–25%, 15–20% and 15–25%**, depending on the service. On a RM30 order, that is between RM4.50 and RM7.50.

husnieats pays **nothing per order**. There is no gateway, because the money moves bank-to-bank by QR. The cost is a person reading a receipt, which is the honest trade: at three dishes and a handful of orders a day, a human check is cheaper and more flexible than an integration. At fifty orders a day it would be the bottleneck, and the answer would be a gateway with a per-transaction fee.

So the claim is narrow and testable: **order taking, ticketing and payment reconciliation can be built and run by one person, at a fraction of a commission, with nothing but a domain, a host and a phone.**

## What it does not do

- **No cards.** If a customer only has a card, this shop cannot take the order. That is a real limit, not a design preference.
- **No rider network.** Delivery is arranged, not dispatched at scale.
- **No team.** The admin is one person's dashboard, not a back office for ten staff.
- **No automatic reconciliation.** Someone has to match the receipt to the order. The system makes that quick; it does not make it disappear.

Naming these is the point. A demonstration that hides its edges is a pitch.

## What it takes to do this yourself

Not much, and less than most people expect:

1. **A place to put it.** A domain and a host. The stack here is deliberately ordinary — a web app and a database, both self-hostable — because the point is reproducibility, not cleverness.
2. **A way to take money.** DuitNow QR costs nothing to display and nothing to receive. A gateway is the upgrade, not the starting point.
3. **A channel for the receipt.** WhatsApp, which your customers already use and already trust.
4. **The discipline.** Write the order down, check the payment, mark it cooking, mark it done. Software does not remove this step; it only makes it faster.

## The same idea at commercial scale

husnieats is a prototype. **mejamakan** is the same shape with a business behind it: a lauk delivery operation in KL and Selangor running its own site, a curated weekly menu grouped by day, accounts on its own domain, "From RM18/meal", Monday-to-Friday delivery, and a plan customers renew — a subscription rather than a one-off order. Their own site reports 3,000+ families served.

Two examples, one small and one trading: an individual can stand up a storefront, and a kitchen can run one commercially. Neither needs a marketplace in the middle to take an order.

## Why this matters more than the commission argument

The commission argument is arithmetic, and arithmetic can be argued with: platforms deliver customers, the fee pays for reach, and at low volume the maths often favours staying put. Fine.

The demonstration is different. It says the capability is no longer the barrier. Ten years ago, taking orders online meant either a marketplace or a developer and a five-figure build. Today it means a domain, a QR code and a weekend — and the only thing left to solve is the part no software sells you, which is getting someone to walk through the door.

**So: the storefront is solved. The audience is the work.**

## Colab will train your model. It will not host it

URL: https://upahje.my/en/articles/colab-hosting-ai-malaysia
Checked: 2026-11-25

The question usually arrives as "how do I host my AI on Colab", and the honest answer is that hosting is the one thing Colab's terms single out. Google's FAQ lists file hosting, media serving and "other web service offerings not related to interactive compute" among the activities disallowed on managed runtimes. A free runtime also blocks remote control: SSH shells and remote desktops, and bypassing the notebook interface to work mainly through a web UI.

That is not a loophole to be worked around with a tunnel. It is the shape of the product.

## What the free tier actually gives you

Colab is a hosted Jupyter notebook with free access to GPUs and TPUs. Notebooks run for at most 12 hours, availability and usage permitting, and the virtual machine is deleted after a period of idleness, with a maximum lifetime the service enforces. Nothing about that is guaranteed: the FAQ says resources are not guaranteed and not unlimited, and that limits fluctuate.

So the free tier is a generous batch machine that resets. It is not a server, and treating it as one produces the three failures below.

## The three failures everyone hits

1. **The tunnel that dies.** Point ngrok or cloudflared at a port inside the notebook and you get a public URL. It lives exactly as long as the VM, which is 12 hours at best and often less. Every restart means a new URL, and nobody who needs your model is going to chase a new link each morning.
2. **The keep-alive script.** A cell that clicks the UI or pings the runtime to defeat the idle timer is the behaviour the FAQ describes as bypassing anti-abuse policy. It also only postpones the 12-hour ceiling.
3. **The secret in the notebook.** Anyone with the link can read every cell, including the API key you pasted to reach a model. This one is not a rule being broken, it is a credential being published.

## What Colab is genuinely good at

It is excellent at the work it was built for, and that work is worth naming precisely:

- **Batch experiments.** Train, evaluate, throw the VM away. A model that takes 40 minutes to fine-tune fits comfortably inside one session.
- **Evaluation harnesses.** Run a fixed case set through a model and score it, with the notebook as the record of what was run.
- **Sharing a method.** A notebook someone can open and execute is a better handover document than a folder of scripts.

The pattern that stays inside the rules: train and tune on Colab, write checkpoints to Drive or object storage, and serve from somewhere designed for serving.

## Where hosting actually lives, with prices

| Option | What it is | Price as printed |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Hugging Face Spaces, CPU Basic | 2 vCPU, 16 GB, a Gradio or Docker app with a permanent URL | free |
| Hugging Face PRO | 8x ZeroGPU quota, higher queue priority, Docker and Gradio Spaces | USD 9/month, about RM37.04 |
| Runpod, per hour | A GPU you start and stop; billed per second | USD 0.27/hr for an RTX A5000, about RM1.11 |
| A local machine | Your own hardware behind a tunnel | hardware plus electricity |

The free Spaces tier is the part most people miss: a small model with a modest request rate does not need a GPU at all, and a permanent URL costs nothing while it does. The RM37.04 for PRO is roughly three hours of an H100 PCIe on a rented platform, which puts the trade in plain terms: a month of hosting against an afternoon of training.

## A workflow that stays inside the rules

1. Do the training and evaluation on Colab, and check the run fits in a session with room to spare.
2. Save the weights to Drive or a model hub the moment a run improves, because the VM will not warn you.
3. Serve from Spaces, a rented GPU, or your own machine, whichever matches the request rate.
4. Keep tokens in notebook secrets or environment variables that are never printed in a cell.
5. Re-read the provider's restricted-activities list before you build a product on top of a free tier, because the list is the contract.

The confusion is not technical, it is about what a notebook is for. Colab sells spare interactive compute to people who are experimenting, and a served product is the opposite of an experiment, so the free tier spends its generosity on training and has none left for hosting.

- Google Colaboratory FAQ (free access to GPUs and TPUs, notebooks run at most 12 hours, restricted activities including file hosting, media serving, SSH shells and remote desktops on free runtimes) — https://research.google.com/colaboratory/faq.html (checked 2026-11-25)
- Hugging Face pricing (Spaces CPU Basic free at 2 vCPU and 16 GB, PRO USD 9/month with 8x ZeroGPU quota) — https://huggingface.co/pricing (checked 2026-11-25)
- Runpod pricing (RTX A5000 USD 0.27/hr, H100 PCIe USD 2.89/hr) for rented serving capacity — https://www.runpod.io/pricing (checked 2026-11-25)

## EPF contribution: 12% or 13%, and RM5,000 is the line

URL: https://upahje.my/en/articles/epf-employer-rate-malaysia
Checked: 2026-11-25

An employer pays 13% of monthly wages when the wage is RM5,000 or less, and 12% when it is more. The employee pays 11% at both levels. The ringgit amount on the payslip is not that multiplication, though: it comes from the Third Schedule and is rounded up to the next ringgit.

## The split happens at RM5,000 exactly

RM5,000 is inside the 13% band, because the rule reads "RM5,000 and below". One ringgit above it moves the employer to 12%, which is why a small raise can cost the employer less than a small raise at the boundary suggests.

The table applies the published percentages to five wages so the break is visible. The last column matters more than the others: the schedule amount is what gets paid.

| Monthly wage | Employer rate | Employer amount at the rate | Employee amount at 11% |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| RM2,000 | 13% | RM260.00 | RM220.00 |
| RM4,999 | 13% | RM649.87 | RM549.89 |
| RM5,000 | 13% | RM650.00 | RM550.00 |
| RM5,001 | 12% | RM600.12 | RM550.11 |
| RM6,000 | 12% | RM720.00 | RM660.00 |

The employee's 11% does not move at RM5,000; only the employer's rate does, so a wage just above the line does not reduce take-home pay.

Those amounts are arithmetic at the published rate, not the schedule. KWSP computes contributions from the Third Schedule for wages up to RM20,000, and the schedule total is rounded up to the next ringgit, so expect the payslip to differ by a few sen.

## Two bands that change the answer

Employees aged 60 and over sit in Part E of the schedule: the employer pays 4% and the employee pays nothing. Non-Malaysian employees have been inside the mandatory scheme since October 2025, in Part F, at 2% employer and 2% employee. Both are schedule amounts, not multiplications. The schedule itself was revised with effect from October 2025, so a table printed before that date is not the one to use.

Neither band appears in a payroll template built for a young all-Malaysian team, which is how a first payslip for a returning retiree goes wrong.

## The deadline is the 15th

Contributions are due on or before the 15th of the following month. KWSP's own example is January wages, February contribution month, paid by 15 February.

Late payment is a different charge from the contribution itself, and this article does not estimate it. Keep proof of payment every month, because disputes usually arrive months later.

## What the boundary costs in a month

At RM5,000 the employer pays RM650.00 at the rate. At RM5,001 the employer pays RM600.12, because the whole wage moves to the 12% band rather than the excess above RM5,000.

That is a RM49.88 drop for a RM1 raise, and it is the one place where paying someone more can cost the business less in EPF. The schedule smooths some of the gap, but the band change is real.

Over a year at a constant wage the gap is RM598.56, and that figure is arithmetic on the published percentages rather than a schedule amount. The Third Schedule is what actually gets paid, and it rounds up to the next ringgit, so the payslip lands within a few sen of these numbers instead of exactly on them.

One more edge: above RM20,000 a month, KWSP stops using the schedule and the exact percentage applies, which is the only band where the multiplication on the page is the amount paid. A payroll template that only knows the schedule will need a second rule for the highest salaries.

## The 60-plus line, worked once

For an employee aged 60 or over at RM3,000, Part E puts the employer rate at 4%; the schedule entry for that wage is RM120, and the employee contributes nothing. The same wage under the 13/11 pair costs the employer RM390 and the employee RM330.

The difference is not a rounding error; it is a band, and it is decided by the employee's age on the contribution month, not by the payroll template's default. A template built for a young team will miss this line until someone checks it by hand.

## What to do before the first payslip

1. Find the wage in the Third Schedule, not on a calculator.
2. Round up to the next ringgit as the schedule does.
3. Pay by the 15th of the following month.
4. Check whether anyone on the payroll is 60 or over, or a non-Malaysian, before using the 13/11 pair.
5. Keep the schedule version you used, because a rate change does not rewrite history.

The 12-versus-13 question is the easy half. The half that costs money is the schedule and the two exceptions, because those are the lines a template gets wrong quietly, and a payroll error is discovered by an employee, not by an auditor.

[More definitions, explained plainly](https://upahje.my/en/glossary)

### Sources

- KWSP, employer mandatory contribution (13% and 12% bands, employee 11%, Third Schedule, 15th-of-the-month payment, Part E) — https://www.kwsp.gov.my/en/employer/responsibilities/mandatory-contribution (checked 2026-11-24)
- KWSP, EPF Act 1991 Third Schedule (contribution rates effective October 2025) — https://www.kwsp.gov.my/documents/d/guest/third_schedule_from_-1-october-2025 (checked 2026-11-25)
- KWSP, contribution for non-Malaysian citizen employees (2% employer, 2% employee, from the October 2025 salary) — https://www.kwsp.gov.my/en/employer/responsibilities/non-malaysian-citizen-employees (checked 2026-11-25)

## The same H100 rents for RM11.89 an hour, or RM7.12

URL: https://upahje.my/en/articles/gpu-rental-cost-malaysia
Checked: 2026-11-25

An Nvidia H100 SXM rents for USD 4.39 an hour on Runpod and from USD 1.73 on Vast.ai. At the reference rate of RM4.1155 to the dollar, that is RM18.07 against RM7.12 for the same model of card. Nothing about the hardware differs. The price differs because one marketplace sells a reservation and the other sells whatever a stranger's machine happens to be idle.

## The published rates, converted

Runpod publishes a fixed card per model. Vast publishes a floor and a median, because each listing is a different host with a different reliability record. Both are quoted below in dollars as printed, then in ringgit at the 24 November 2026 rate.

| Card | Runpod, as printed | In ringgit | Vast from | In ringgit | Vast median |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| H100 SXM, 80 GB | USD 4.39/hr | RM18.07 | USD 1.73/hr | RM7.12 | USD 2.40/hr |
| H100 PCIe, 80 GB | USD 2.89/hr | RM11.89 | USD 2.31/hr | RM9.51 | USD 2.53/hr |
| H100 NVL, 94 GB | USD 3.19/hr | RM13.13 | USD 2.57/hr | RM10.58 | — |
| B200, 180 GB | USD 7.99/hr | RM32.88 | — | — | — |
| RTX A5000, 24 GB | USD 0.27/hr | RM1.11 | — | — | — |

The H100 PCIe row is the interesting one: the gap narrows from 2.5 times to 1.25 times the moment you compare the same variant rather than the flagship. A firm that prices a project off the fastest card on one platform and the cheapest card on another is comparing two different products.

## Per-second billing is where the money actually moves

Runpod bills per second on its secure cloud, and Vast bills to the second with no minimum hours. That matters more than the headline rate for work that finishes early, because a training run that ends after 18 minutes should not cost an hour.

An 18-minute run on an H100 PCIe at RM11.89 an hour comes to RM3.57. The same run bought in whole hours costs RM11.89, and the difference across twenty experiments is RM166 rather than RM714.

## A month of continuous rent, in ringgit

Nobody runs an H100 continuously to serve a small business, but the monthly figure is the one that ends the argument about buying a card. At 720 hours:

| Configuration | Monthly, in ringgit |
| --- | --- |
| Vast H100 SXM at the floor | RM5,126 |
| Vast H100 SXM at the median | RM7,114 |
| Runpod H100 PCIe | RM8,561 |
| Runpod H100 SXM | RM13,010 |
| Runpod B200 | RM23,674 |

A single H100 card bought outright costs more than a year of the cheapest monthly rent above, before power, cooling and the fact that it is obsolete the moment the next generation ships. That arithmetic is the whole case for renting, and it holds at every row in the table.

## What the cheap listings cost you

The floor price on a marketplace is a machine in someone's data centre, and the listing tells you which. Check three things before running anything with a deadline:

1. **Interruptible or not.** The lowest rates are usually preemptible, which means the job stops when the host needs the card back.
2. **Network speed.** A cheap card behind a slow link is the wrong tool for anything that moves a dataset.
3. **Verification and reliability score.** A host with a short track record is cheaper for a reason, and an interrupted 6-hour run costs more than the difference in rate.

Runpod's fixed price buys a known card and a known region. Vast's floor buys capacity somebody else did not want this hour. Both are legitimate purchases; they are not the same purchase.

## What to do before you rent anything

1. Price the same card variant on both platforms, not the flagship on one and the budget card on the other.
2. Convert at a rate you can cite, and write the date next to it, because a ringgit figure without a date is a rumour.
3. Estimate the run in minutes, not hours, and check whether billing is per second.
4. For anything with a deadline, price the interruptible rate out of the comparison entirely.

The ringgit figure that matters for a Malaysian business is not the hourly rate, it is the cost of the experiment that fails. At RM7 an hour you can afford to be wrong four times on a Saturday, and that is worth more than a guarantee of the fastest card.

- Vast.ai, GPU pricing (H100 SXM from USD 1.73/hr, median USD 2.40/hr; H100 PCIe from USD 2.31/hr; billed to the second, no minimum hours) — https://vast.ai/pricing (checked 2026-11-25)

## HRD Corp levy: 1%, 0.5%, or none

URL: https://upahje.my/en/articles/hrd-corp-levy-malaysia
Checked: 2026-11-25

A business with ten or more Malaysian employees pays 1% of monthly wages to HRD Corp. At five to nine employees the same levy is optional, at 0.5%. Below five there is no levy, a position the bands imply rather than print, and a first hire therefore carries nothing.

## The levy starts at five, and becomes compulsory at ten

The registered-employers page states that for employers with 10 or more Malaysian employees the levy is compulsory at 1% of monthly wages, and that employers with 5 to 9 are given the option to register at 0.5%.

A business with four employees is not named in either band. It sits below both, which is why a first hire carries no levy at all and why the total cost of that hire is the statutory trio and not a quartet. If the headcount is approaching five, treat the levy as starting before you hire, not after.

## What the levy is charged on

The percentage applies to the monthly wages of employees, so the ringgit figure is a share of payroll rather than a flat fee per head. The table below uses an average monthly wage of RM3,000 as a stated assumption, so a reader can substitute their own payroll and read the rate column, which is the sourced part.

| Malaysian employees | Rate | Monthly levy at RM3,000 average wage | Annual levy |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 4 | none | RM0 | RM0 |
| 5 | 0.5% | RM75 | RM900 |
| 9 | 0.5% | RM135 | RM1,620 |
| 10 | 1% | RM300 | RM3,600 |
| 25 | 1% | RM750 | RM9,000 |

The jump from nine to ten is the expensive one: the rate doubles and the headcount that crosses the line adds its own wage to the base in the same month.

## What changes at the boundary

A business at nine employees on a RM3,000 average wage pays RM135 a month. Hiring the tenth moves it to RM300, so the tenth salary costs the employer the wage, the statutory add-ons and an extra RM165 a month of levy.

Annualised, the step from nine to ten is RM1,980 in levy alone at that average wage, before the new employee's own EPF, SOCSO, EIS and any LINDUNG 24 Jam deduction.

## Registration runs on Form 1, and review is 30 days

A company at ten Malaysian employees or more fills Form 1 — the page words the threshold as "more than 10" while the levy itself starts at ten — and the page states that the application is reviewed by officers within 30 days. That review window is the only timing the page prints, so treat 30 days as a review period rather than a deadline you can plan a payroll around.

## No due date is printed

The registered-employers page does not state when the levy must be paid. That is an absence, not a gap to fill with a guessed date, so no payment deadline appears in this article. A business that needs the date should ask HRD Corp or read the levy rules rather than trust a template.

## What to do before the headcount moves

1. Count Malaysian employees only, because the bands are written that way.
2. Check whether you are at four, five or ten, since each is a different regime.
3. Register on Form 1 before assuming the 30-day review protects you.
4. Recalculate the month the tenth hire starts, not the month after.
5. Ask HRD Corp for the payment date in writing, because the page does not print one.

The levy is small enough to ignore and large enough to notice at the ten-employee line, which is exactly the moment a business stops checking. Budgeting it at nine employees and discovering it at ten is a RM3,600-a-year surprise at a RM3,000 average wage, and that surprise lands in a month that is already busy with a new hire.

### Sources

- PSMB Act 2001, section 15: levy on an employer who opts to be registered (the 0.5% option) — https://www.mylaw.my/akta/pembangunan-sumber-manusia-berhad-2001/section-15 (checked 2026-11-25)
- HRD Corp, registered employers (1% compulsory at 10 or more Malaysian employees, 0.5% optional at 5 to 9, Form 1 reviewed within 30 days) — https://hrdcorp.gov.my/registered-employers (checked 2026-11-24)

## POS: RM122 a month, and no free tier files e-invoice

URL: https://upahje.my/en/articles/pos-system-cost-malaysia
Checked: 2026-11-25

A POS subscription in Malaysia starts at RM122 a month on StoreHub and runs to RM235 for the next tier, while Qashier charges RM8 a day for the platform plus RM1 to RM3 a day per terminal. None of the free POS tiers is documented as MyInvois-compliant; the RM0 plan that does document LHDN e-Invoice is Bukku, and it is accounting software, not a till.

## The published prices, as printed

StoreHub's Malaysian page prints Starter from RM122 a month and Advanced from RM235. Qashier prices by the day rather than the month, and offers a 24-month route at RM4,580 once.

That difference matters when you compare a monthly card against a daily one, so the table normalises nothing and shows each vendor's own unit.

| Vendor and plan | Price as printed | Terminal hardware | LHDN e-invoice on the pricing page |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| StoreHub Starter | From RM122/month | no hardware price printed | not stated |
| StoreHub Advanced | From RM235/month | no hardware price printed | not stated |
| Qashier, software only | RM8/day | your own phone, tablet or terminal | not stated |
| Qashier with a terminal | RM8 + RM1 (XS) / RM2 (X2) / RM3 (XL SLIM) a day | included, nothing upfront | not stated |
| Qashier, paid upfront | RM4,580 once for 24 months, save RM1,260 | platform only | not stated |
| Bukku Launch, accounting not POS | RM0/month, free forever | not a till | yes, it supports LHDN e-Invoice |

The last column is deliberately empty for two of the three vendors: neither StoreHub nor Qashier states e-invoice support on the pricing page read here, so nothing is claimed for them. Qashier's prices also exclude SST, which the page prints.

## What the subscription does not include

The two vendors handle hardware in opposite ways. StoreHub's pricing page carries no hardware figures at all, so a terminal, a drawer and a receipt printer arrive as separate lines in a quote. Qashier folds the terminal into the daily rate: RM1 a day for the compact XS, RM2 for the X2, RM3 for the XL SLIM, nothing upfront, with the hardware owned after two years.

A shop that budgets RM122 for software and RM0 for hardware has budgeted half a till. Ask whether the quote is rent, purchase or lease, because the three end at different 24-month totals, and note that Qashier's daily figure carries on for as long as the shop keeps paying it.

## Why the POS e-invoice question is the expensive one

A till that is not wired to MyInvois leaves the filing to whoever does the books, and that is the manual retyping the whole exercise is meant to remove. A POS that is documented as compliant is worth a higher monthly fee than a cheaper till plus a worker typing invoices twice.

The free plan that does document e-Invoice is Bukku's Launch, and it is an accounting product with 100 MB of storage and 100 emails a month. It files e-invoices; it does not take payment at a counter or print a receipt, and that difference decides whether it is a solution for your shop or only for your bookkeeping.

## Do the daily prices add up to the monthly ones

Qashier at RM8 a day is about RM243 over a 30-day month before terminals, so the daily card is not automatically cheaper than StoreHub's RM122. It becomes cheaper when the shop opens fewer days than it pays for, which is a calendar question rather than a software one.

The RM4,580 for 24 months works out at about RM191 a month, which sits between the two StoreHub tiers and above Qashier's own daily rate at a full month.

## What to ask before signing

1. Is e-invoice compliance in the plan you quoted, in writing?
2. Does the price include the terminal, or is hardware separate?
3. What happens to the subscription if you close for a week?
4. Does the plan file to MyInvois directly, or export a file someone uploads?
5. What is the 24-month total, not the monthly headline?

Pay for the e-invoice route, not the till. A POS that takes money but leaves the invoice to a person is a counter with a subscription, and the subscription is the smaller cost of the two.

## SOCSO stops at RM6,000

URL: https://upahje.my/en/articles/socso-employer-rate-malaysia
Checked: 2026-11-25

An employer pays 1.75% of monthly wages into SOCSO and deducts 0.5% from the employee, up to a wage ceiling of RM6,000 that took effect on 1 October 2024. EIS is 0.2% each side, on the same ceiling. Above RM6,000 every one of those lines is flat, so a raise costs the employer nothing extra in SOCSO or EIS.

## The rate follows the wage until the ceiling

Below RM6,000 the contribution is a percentage of the wage, and at RM6,000 it stops moving. The table applies the published rates to four wages; the schedule amounts differ by a few sen because SOCSO is table-based, not flat arithmetic.

| Monthly wage | Employer SOCSO at 1.75% | Employee SOCSO at 0.5% | EIS each side at 0.2% |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| RM3,000 | RM52.50 | RM15.00 | RM6.00 |
| RM5,999 | RM104.98 | RM30.00 | RM12.00 |
| RM6,000 | RM105.00 | RM30.00 | RM12.00 |
| RM8,000 | RM105.00 | RM30.00 | RM12.00 |

The last two rows are the point. A RM2,000 raise costs the employer nothing in SOCSO and nothing in EIS, which is why the cap matters more to a senior hire than to a junior one.

## Two categories, and the one that covers injury only

First Category, for employees under 60, covers both the employment injury scheme and the invalidity scheme at 1.75% employer and 0.5% employee.

Second Category, for employees aged 60 and over, is the injury scheme only: 1.25% payable by the employer, with no employee share.

Putting a 60-year-old on the First Category row overpays; putting a 25-year-old on the Second Category row leaves them uncovered for invalidity. Both mistakes are silent on a payslip and only surface when a claim is made.

## EIS is separate, and smaller

EIS is 0.4% in total, split 0.2% employer and 0.2% employee, and it shares the RM6,000 ceiling. It is not SOCSO and it does not appear in a SOCSO table, which is why payroll summaries that show one line for "SOCSO/EIS" hide which scheme a ringgit went to.

## What the cap is worth at two wages

At RM4,500 the employer pays RM78.75 in SOCSO. At RM7,500 the employer pays RM105.00, which is 1.4%, and the employee pays RM30.00, which is 0.4% rather than the headline 0.5%.

The percentage printed on a rate card is a rate up to the ceiling, not a rate on every salary, and that is why the calculation on a high salary has to stop at RM6,000. A quotation that multiplies 1.75% by a RM9,000 salary overstates the SOCSO line by RM52.50 a month, and the same mistake on EIS overstates it by RM6.00.

## What is not confirmed here

Registration timing is deliberately not printed here: PERKESO's employer-registration page was outside what we verified for this article, so no deadline appears. Employers still have to register, and that date should be confirmed with PERKESO before the first payroll month rather than after it.

Schedule amounts are also not reproduced: the table applies the percentages, and PERKESO's schedule is authoritative for the ringgit figures. If the payslip differs from your arithmetic, the schedule is right and the calculator is wrong.

## What to do before the first payslip

1. Put each employee in the right category before anything else.
2. Apply the percentage up to RM6,000 and stop there.
3. Keep EIS on its own line, because it is a different scheme.
4. Check the schedule for the exact amount, and expect a few sen difference.
5. Confirm the registration deadline at PERKESO directly before the first payroll.

The ceiling is the only part of this that changes how you hire. Below RM6,000 the contribution tracks the salary, but above it the scheme is a fixed cost, so the marginal cost of a senior hire is lower than a payroll spreadsheet suggests, and the marginal cost of a junior one is higher.

- PERKESO, contribution rate (RM6,000 wage ceiling effective 1 October 2024) — https://www.perkeso.gov.my/en/our-services/employer-employee/kadar-caruman.html (checked 2026-11-25)

## A spare laptop is a server only after you measure it

URL: https://upahje.my/en/articles/spare-laptop-home-server-malaysia
Checked: 2026-11-25

A laptop that is already in a drawer costs nothing to acquire, which is why the idea appeals: one service, no monthly fee, no cloud account. The catch is that "free hardware" is a statement about purchase price, and running a machine for a year is a statement about electricity, uptime and your own evenings.

None of that is a reason to avoid it. It is a reason to do four measurements before you commit an evening to it.

## What it actually draws

Modern laptops idle low. A machine with the lid shut, no display output and one service listening will sit somewhere between a nightlight and a light bulb, and the only number that counts is the one your meter shows.

The label on the power brick does not tell you. It states the maximum the adapter can deliver, not what the machine consumes at rest, and the two differ by a factor of five or more.

A plug-in power meter costs about RM30 at any hardware shop, and it converts the whole decision from an argument into a reading. Run the laptop at idle for an hour with the service up, write the watt figure down, and use that.

## The arithmetic, with assumptions stated

Take 20 watts at idle — a plausible figure for a laptop serving one lightweight service — and a domestic rate of 45 sen per kWh. Both are assumptions, and you should replace both with your own.

- 20 W for 24 hours is 480 Wh, or 0.48 kWh a day.
- At 45 sen, that is about 21.6 sen a day.
- Over a year, 175 kWh, or about RM79.

Change the wattage and the answer scales with it: 40 W doubles it to about RM158 a year, 10 W halves it to about RM40. The tariff you should use is printed in your own bill, and TNB publishes the domestic schedule if the bill is not clear enough.

Compare that with the cheapest monthly rent that does the same job. A small cloud instance is often around RM20 to RM40 a month, which is RM240 to RM480 a year. The laptop wins on money at any of the wattages above, and it stops winning the moment your time is priced at more than a few hours a year.

## The battery is not a UPS

A laptop has a built-in battery, and it is tempting to treat that as free protection against a power cut. It is not, for two reasons.

First, a battery that spends its life at 100 per cent and warm degrades quickly, and a swollen battery in a machine running unattended is a fire risk rather than an inconvenience. Most laptops let you cap charging at 60 to 80 per cent in firmware, and a self-hosted machine should.

Second, a graceful shutdown is worth more than five minutes of runtime. Set the machine to shut down when the battery hits a threshold, and assume the power will go out while you are away.

## What to install, and what to skip

1. **A server distribution, not a desktop.** Ubuntu Server or Debian, no graphical session. A desktop environment on a headless machine is memory you are paying for and an attack surface you are not using.
2. **The lid behaviour, set explicitly.** Most laptops suspend when the lid closes, which is the opposite of what a server should do.
3. **`systemd` units with restart policies**, so a service that dies comes back without you.
4. **One way in, not three.** Tailscale or a Cloudflare tunnel gives you remote access without opening a port on the router, and neither needs a static IP.
5. **A backup that leaves the machine.** A server with one copy of its data on one disk is a scheduled loss, whatever the uptime.

Skip the RAID conversation. Two disks in a laptop is rare, and a backup elsewhere solves the problem RAID does not.

## Where this stops working

A spare laptop is the right answer for a personal service, a small internal tool, or a place to run scheduled jobs. It is the wrong answer for anything a customer depends on, for three reasons that no amount of configuration fixes:

- **Residential power and internet.** Both fail, and neither comes with an SLA.
- **A dynamic address.** Tunnels solve reachability, not reliability.
- **One machine, no redundancy.** When it dies, it is down until you are home.

If the service matters to someone else, the RM240 a year for a small instance is the cheapest part of the decision.

## The order to do it in

1. Measure idle watts with a meter, with the service running.
2. Read your own tariff, then calculate the year.
3. Compare it against a small cloud instance at the same workload.
4. Cap the battery charge and set a shutdown threshold.
5. Install a server distribution, set lid behaviour, and add one tunnel.
6. Point a backup at storage outside the machine before you trust it with anything.

That sequence takes an evening and produces a number rather than an opinion, which is the difference between a hobby and a decision.

### Sources

- Tenaga Nasional Berhad, residential pricing and tariffs (the domestic tariff schedule a household reads to find its own per-kWh rate) — https://www.tnb.com.my/residential/pricing-tariffs (checked 2026-11-25)
- Ubuntu Server, system requirements and installation guide for a spare machine — https://ubuntu.com/server/docs/installation (checked 2026-11-25)
