## A trading bot is a data problem wearing a model's clothes

URL: https://upahje.my/en/articles/trading-bot-reality-malaysia
Checked: 2026-11-25

A reinforcement-learning agent trained on nine FX and cryptocurrency symbols finished its full run in 17.9 minutes on rented GPU time, for USD 0.14. It then made exactly one decision per symbol, over and over: hold, or sell, whichever the reward gradient found first. That outcome is not a training bug. It is the honest answer to a badly posed question, and it is the outcome most bot projects reach after a year of buying better hardware.

## The cheap part was the training

Nine symbols, 17.9 minutes, USD 0.14. At Runpod's listed H100 SXM rate of USD 4.39 an hour, a run of that length costs less than a cup of coffee, and cheaper listings of the same card exist elsewhere. Compute is not the constraint and has not been for years. Anyone who tells you their bot needs a bigger GPU is describing a data problem they have not diagnosed.

The constraint is that a model cannot learn an edge that is not in the data it was given. Feed it six months of minute candles and it will learn the shape of six months of minute candles, including every accident that happened to be in those months.

## What the collapse actually says

A policy that outputs the same action for every input has found the lowest-variance policy available. In a market series where most timesteps look alike, that is often the rational move: the reward signal barely distinguishes one action from another, so the gradient settles on the safest constant.

The fix is not a bigger network or a longer run. It is either a reward that separates good decisions from bad ones at the resolution you actually trade at, or an acceptance that the signal is too thin for a learned policy and a rule belongs there instead. Both answers are cheaper than another GPU and both are harder to accept.

## The part that did work was arithmetic

Where the same research did produce a usable edge, the method was not a model. It was a defined rule measured across six months of funding-rate data: when the funding rate sat above its own 90th percentile, the following periods produced 60 to 70 per cent win rates at 55 to 77 basis points per holding period, with venue fees and funding costs applied rather than assumed away.

That result has four properties a neural network does not give you. It is explainable in one sentence. It is measurable on a sample. It fails visibly when the regime changes. And it can be checked by someone who does not trust you.

## Four gates before any strategy gets money

A backtest is not evidence. These are the gates used before a strategy was allowed to move past paper:

1. **Win rate above 50 per cent** on the full window, not on the best month.
2. **Profit factor above 1.2**, so the wins are large enough to survive a losing run.
3. **At least 20 trades**, because ten trades is an anecdote with a chart.
4. **Survival across the whole window**, including the months the strategy did nothing.

Add decay measurement — how long an edge lasted, not just whether it appeared — and a strategy that passes all four is still only a candidate. Paper trading comes next, and it is not optional, because slippage and fills are where backtests die.

## What this costs a small operator

The honest budget for a bot that might work is not the subscription. It is the months of data work before the first trade: getting clean price series, modelling fees at the venue you will actually use, and writing the validation harness that stops you deploying the version that looked good in March.

Most projects skip that and buy the model instead. That is why they end with a chart that goes up in the past and a live account that does not.

## Where to start, if you are starting

1. Pick one instrument and one rule you can state in a sentence.
2. Get six months of data from the venue's own API, not from a screenshot.
3. Apply fees and funding before you look at the result, not after.
4. Write the four gates down before you see the numbers, so you cannot move them afterwards.
5. Paper trade for a month, and record fills rather than prices.

The bot is the easy part to build and the easiest part to be wrong about. The work that decides whether it makes money happens before a single order is sent, in a spreadsheet most people skip because it is not as interesting as the training loop.

## Grab and foodpanda commission rates (2026)

URL: https://upahje.my/en/articles/delivery-commission-malaysia
Checked: 2026-11-25

Neither Grab nor foodpanda prints a merchant commission on any page a business can read. The only citable commission figures in Malaysia come from the competition regulator's own foodpanda decision, in bands from 1% to 25%, and at the top of that band a RM25 order leaves RM8.50 before labour, rent or electricity.

## The platforms publish nothing

Grab's Malaysian merchant page sells the programme and prints no rate: the word commission does not appear in the served text, and there is no rate card on the page. foodpanda's merchant page returned HTTP 403 to this client, so its rate is not readable at all.

That matters because the common sentence in Malaysian guides, that GrabFood takes a certain percentage, is not a published rate. It is a merchant's contract, a vendor's estimate, or folklore, and none of those can be checked by a reader deciding whether to sign.

## The regulator's numbers are bands, and the names are redacted

The MyCC decision on foodpanda records five anonymised franchised merchants with commission bands: 1% to 5%, 10% to 25%, 15% to 20%, and twice 15% to 25%. The merchant names are redacted, which tells you the actual rates are contractual and confidential.

The decision also records the finding that foodpanda "imposes higher commission rates on independent restaurants than on franchised restaurants due to a disparity in bargaining power". The Commission found no infringement, so this is a description of the market, not a penalty.

The decision itself is dated 11 September 2023; the case list carries 13 September 2023, which is the date the press reported it.

## What the top of the band costs on a real basket

The arithmetic below applies the 25% upper edge and a 20% midpoint, with packaging at RM1.50 per order and food cost at 35% of menu price. Packaging and food cost are assumptions, not published figures; commission is the regulator's band.

| Basket | Commission at 25% | Commission at 20% | Packaging | Net after commission and packaging, at 25% / 20% | Food cost at 35% | Left before labour and rent, at 25% / 20% |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| RM15 | RM3.75 | RM3.00 | RM1.50 | RM9.75 / RM10.50 | RM5.25 | RM4.50 / RM5.25 |
| RM25 | RM6.25 | RM5.00 | RM1.50 | RM17.25 / RM18.50 | RM8.75 | RM8.50 / RM9.75 |
| RM45 | RM11.25 | RM9.00 | RM1.50 | RM32.25 / RM34.50 | RM15.75 | RM16.50 / RM18.75 |

Each row subtracts commission, then packaging, then food cost, in that order, so a reader can redo any cell with a calculator. Read the last column as what is left to pay for the cook, the rent and the gas. On a RM15 order at the top of the band it is RM4.50, which is not a margin; it is a warning that small baskets carry fixed costs badly.

The 35% food cost is the weakest number here, and it is ours. A business with a different food cost should redo the row with its own figure, which is why it is in a column of its own rather than folded into a total.

## What is not published

Promo co-funding: neither platform states whether the merchant funds part of a platform promotion, or at what share, and the MyCC decision references a promotional-expense spreadsheet whose values are redacted. No percentage is printed here.

Delivery fee: neither platform page states who sets it or who keeps it, so no claim is made about it.

GrabFood's rate: no MyCC decision and no platform page, so there is nothing citable at all.

## What to ask before signing

1. The commission rate in writing, per category, not a range.
2. Whether the rate changes with exclusivity, and what the non-exclusive rate is.
3. Who pays for promotions, and at what share.
4. Who sets the delivery fee and who keeps it.
5. The rate for a small basket, in ringgit, at your menu prices.

A platform that will not put the rate beside a worked basket is telling you something. The honest answer to "what will I keep on a RM25 order" is a number, and a sales page that will not produce it is asking you to sign a contract you cannot price.

## A first hire at RM3,000 costs RM3,448.50 a month

URL: https://upahje.my/en/articles/first-hire-cost-malaysia
Checked: 2026-11-24

A RM3,000 salary costs the business RM3,448.50 a month before any allowance, and the person receives RM2,626.50. The gap is four statutory lines, and one of them is a deduction most payroll templates do not carry: LINDUNG 24 Jam, a cover paid entirely by the employee.

## The employer pays 14.95% above the salary

The employer's share is EPF at 13%, SOCSO at 1.75% and EIS at 0.2% of the wage, because a RM3,000 monthly wage sits below the RM5,000 line where EPF drops to 12%. Those three lines add RM448.50 to the RM3,000.

The employee's side is larger than it looks. EPF takes 11%, SOCSO 0.5%, EIS 0.2%, and LINDUNG 24 Jam another 0.75% in its first phase. That is RM373.50, so the take-home is RM2,626.50.

## Two of the four lines are capped

SOCSO and EIS are capped at an assumed monthly wage of RM6,000, a ceiling that took effect on 1 October 2024. Above that wage the contributions stay flat in ringgit, which makes them proportionally cheaper for a senior hire and proportionally painful for a first hire near the floor.

SOCSO also has a second category: an employer contribution of 1.25% that covers the injury scheme only, for employees aged 60 and over.

## The payslip line most templates miss

LINDUNG 24 Jam covers accidents outside work and not related to the job, around the clock, for eligible employees. The employee pays the whole contribution, which is why it never appears in an employer-cost calculator.

It is phased: 0.75% for the first two years, 1.0% for the next three, and 1.25% from the sixth year. Employees already on the payroll stayed in the scheme unless they opted out during the window that ran from 13 July to 31 August 2026.

A first hire joining today does not get that window. PERKESO's own page states that local employees employed for the first time after 31 August 2026 are required to contribute under SKBBK, so the 0.75% belongs on the payslip from the first month.

## What the RM3,000 hire looks like

| Line | Employer pays | Employee pays |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Gross salary | RM3,000.00 | — |
| EPF 13% / 11% | RM390.00 | RM330.00 |
| SOCSO 1.75% / 0.5% | RM52.50 | RM15.00 |
| EIS 0.2% / 0.2% | RM6.00 | RM6.00 |
| LINDUNG 24 Jam 0.75% | — | RM22.50 |
| Total | RM3,448.50 | RM373.50 |

The percentages are as published, but the ringgit amounts on a real payslip come from the contribution schedule, which is table-based and rounds up to the next ringgit. Expect the schedule to differ from flat arithmetic by a few sen, not by ringgit.

At RM2,000 the same arithmetic gives an employer cost of RM2,299.00 and an employee deduction of RM249.00. The employer share stays at 14.95%, because every line below the ceiling is a flat percentage of the wage.

## Two lines with no number here

The HRD Corp levy starts at five Malaysian employees: optional at five to nine at 0.5%, compulsory at ten at 1%, with Form 1 reviewed within 30 days. A first hire sits below both bands, which is why no levy appears in the totals above.

PCB, the monthly tax deduction, is computed from LHDN's MTD schedule. The page read documents the mechanism, the free submission channels and the payment routes, and it gives no remittance due date; anyone quoting a date for it is citing the MTD rules, not that page. The take-home figures above are before tax, and this article does not estimate a tax number.

## What to do before the first payslip

1. Register the employer with EPF and PERKESO before the first salary month, not after it.
2. Pay the contribution on or before the 15th of the following month; the KWSP page's own example is January salary, February contribution, paid by 15 February.
3. Add LINDUNG 24 Jam to the payslip template at 0.75%, and put the phase change in a calendar note for two years out.
4. Use the schedule amount for SOCSO and EIS, not a flat percentage, and round up as the schedule does.
5. Budget the employer cost, not the salary, when you decide what you can afford to hire.

The salary is the smaller number in this decision. A business that budgets RM3,000 and discovers RM3,448.50 after the offer has already spent the difference on something else, and the first place it cuts is the training the new hire needed.

### Sources

- KWSP, employer mandatory contribution (rates, Third Schedule rounding, 15th-of-the-month payment) — https://www.kwsp.gov.my/en/employer/responsibilities/mandatory-contribution (checked 2026-11-24)
- PERKESO, contributions (EPF-adjacent scope, EIS, registration) — https://www.perkeso.gov.my/en/our-services/employer-employee/contributions.html (checked 2026-11-24)
- PERKESO, contribution rate (SOCSO 1.75%/0.5%, RM6,000 ceiling, second category) — https://www.perkeso.gov.my/en/our-services/employer-employee/kadar-caruman.html (checked 2026-11-24)
- PERKESO, LINDUNG 24 Jam (employee-borne, phased rates, SKBBK for new hires after 31 August 2026) — https://www.perkeso.gov.my/en/our-services/protection/lindung-24-jam.html (checked 2026-11-24)
- HRD Corp, registered employers (levy thresholds, 0.5% and 1%, Form 1 review) — https://hrdcorp.gov.my/registered-employers (checked 2026-11-24)
- LHDN, monthly tax deduction page (mechanism and channels, no remittance date) — https://www.hasil.gov.my/en/majikan/pembayaran-pcb/ (checked 2026-11-24)

## Two free tools against OpusClip: the Malay caption gap

URL: https://upahje.my/en/articles/self-hosted-clipping
Checked: 2026-11-24

OpusClip's Starter plan is USD 15 a month, which is RM61.78 at Bank Negara's middle rate of 4.1185 on 24 November 2026, and no Malaysian publisher prints a ringgit price for a clipping subscription at all. Two MIT-licensed repos that appeared in the same week clip on your own machine for nothing, and neither has demonstrated a Malay caption.

## The subscription is priced in dollars

OpusClip prints "USD 15/mo" for Starter and sells it monthly only. That is the only unambiguous price on the page read; the Pro tier sits behind a yearly/monthly toggle and a pack selector, and its figure was not captured as a static number.

The ringgit figure above is a conversion, not a Malaysian price. No publisher selling clipping subscriptions to Malaysians printed one on any page read, and presenting a converted dollar as a local price is how a RM45 subscription turns into RM62 in a budget.

## Two repos arrived in the same week

`neonclipping` was created on 19 November 2026 and has 2,313 stars as of 24 November 2026: MIT, Python, "paste a link, get captioned 9:16 clips in about two minutes". `PeakCut` was created on 14 November 2026 and has 1,848 stars as of 24 November 2026: MIT, Python, self-hosted, bring your own AI key.

Both are young, both are moving, and both are already past the star counts that circulated when they launched, which is a reminder that a star count is true for the minute it is read: `neonclipping` moved by one between the packet and this check.

## What the free path costs instead

A machine with a GPU, the electricity, and an evening to install and tune it. neonclipping's own measured table reports 97 seconds to clip an 85-minute stream in Fast mode, on one machine with an RTX 2060 and 16 threads.

That figure is the author's machine, not yours and not a Malaysian laptop's. A slower card means a longer wait, and no test of either repo on Malaysian hardware exists.

## The numbers, side by side

| Item | OpusClip Starter | neonclipping | PeakCut |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Price as printed | USD 15/month | 0 | 0 |
| Ringgit per month, converted at 4.1185 | 61.78 | 0 | 0 |
| Licence fee | n/a | 0, MIT | 0, MIT |
| Time per clip, as published | not printed | 97 s for an 85-minute stream | not printed |
| GitHub stars, as of 24 November 2026 | n/a | 2,313 | 1,848 |
| Malay captions demonstrated | n/a | unproven | English only |

The two zeroes are licence costs, not total costs. Your time and the machine are real, and the table cannot price them for you.

## Where the free path breaks

**Malay captions.** neonclipping claims 52 caption languages through Whisper and does not name Malay among them, and publishes no Malay sample or accuracy figure. PeakCut "hears English by default" and states that "captions on the clips are in English", with Arabic as the only documented non-English path. If your audience reads captions in Malay, neither repo has shown you it works.

**What the model can see.** neonclipping's own limits section says the local LLM "sees text only; it cannot see the screen", and its optional visual review is off by default and can add CPU time. PeakCut clips by loudness when no key is supplied.

## The volume where cancelling pays

The arithmetic: RM61.78 buys four clips a month at RM15.45 each, eight at RM7.72, and twelve at RM5.15. The free path's marginal cost is 97 seconds of GPU per 85-minute source, so twelve clips cost about nineteen minutes of machine time for the month.

Twelve clips is the number I would use, and it is a judgement rather than a sourced finding. Below it, you are paying RM5 to RM15 a clip for convenience; above it, the free path's cost is fixed and the subscription buys nothing you cannot do on the machine you already own.

The instalment is one evening either way. That is the real cost on the free side, and it is paid once.

## What to count before cancelling

1. Count the clips you published last month, not the ones you meant to.
2. Install one repo on the machine you already own and clip one long video.
3. Watch the output for Malay words if your captions are in Malay; no repo will tell you how good they are.
4. Time the run, and compare that time against RM61.78 of subscription.
5. Decide on the count, not on the demo.

The cheapest mistake here is paying for a year of clips you never post.

### Sources

- OpusClip, pricing (Starter at USD 15 per month, USD only) — https://www.opus.pro/pricing (checked 2026-11-24)
- Bank Negara Malaysia, exchange-rate API (USD middle rate 4.1185) — https://api.bnm.gov.my/public/exchange-rate (checked 2026-11-24)
- iamajmeena/neonclipping, repository (MIT, created 19 November 2026) — https://github.com/iamajmeena/neonclipping (checked 2026-11-24)
- haziqahmedqasmi/PeakCut, repository (MIT, created 14 November 2026) — https://github.com/haziqahmedqasmi/PeakCut (checked 2026-11-24)

## CommandCode, OpenCode, DeepSeek: not the same kind of tool

URL: https://upahje.my/en/articles/commandcode-opencode-deepseek-numbers
Checked: 2026-11-23

These are three different kinds of thing, and the words matter before the prices do. `dsh` is DeepSeek Harness, the command-line harness we run here. An "arm" is one of the products tried on the same task, and this run had three: CommandCode, OpenCode and DeepSeek through `dsh`. CommandCode is a paid coding CLI. OpenCode is a free, MIT-licensed coding CLI with an optional subscription. DeepSeek is a model vendor with an API. What follows is what each publishes as a price, where those numbers have moved, and what one run showed. The benchmark half, and the reason a "CommandCode vs OpenCode" score does not exist, is a separate developer note.

## What do the prices look like as published?

CommandCode sells monthly tiers, and every paid tier carries a processing fee with no figure attached.

| Offering | Tier | Price as printed |
| --- | --- | --- |
| CommandCode | Go | $1/month + processing fee, $10 credits included |
| CommandCode | GOAT | $10/month + processing fee, up to $100 in credits |
| CommandCode | Pro | $20/month |
| CommandCode | Max 10× | $100/month + processing fee, $150 credits |
| CommandCode | Provider (API plan) | $15/month + processing fee |
| OpenCode | the agent itself | Free, MIT licence |
| OpenCode | Go | $10/month |
| OpenCode | Go Plus | $40/month |
| OpenCode | Go Teams | $20 per member per month, two-member minimum |
| DeepSeek | deepseek-flash input, cache miss | $0.15 off-peak / $0.30 peak per 1M tokens |
| DeepSeek | deepseek-flash output | $0.60 off-peak / $1.20 peak per 1M tokens |

The processing fee is the line to ask about, because "plus processing fee" is printed on five of the tiers and the fee appears nowhere on the page in a figure or a link.

## Where did the numbers drift?

CommandCode's own offer has moved since August, and both versions are still quotable.

A Hacker News post on **5 August 2026** announced "Command Code GOAT, $10/month for $70 of credits across 30 models". Today's pricing page shows the same $10/month GOAT tier with "up to $100 in credits", and the models page says "All 107" models. Same tier, same price, more credits and more models. That is a normal promotional drift, and it matters because a review written in August is describing an offer that no longer exists.

The lesson is that a dated figure needs its date, or it becomes a claim about today that nobody can check.

The 38.5% figure that circulates for DeepSeek belongs to Terminal-bench 4.1, where it is DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 run under Claude Code, so it is a result for the model inside someone else's harness and not a result for either CLI named here, and it cannot be compared with a SWE-bench figure because the benchmark, the agent and the task set are different.

## What did we run ourselves?

One task, in one harness, printed as a sidebar and not as a head-to-head: `dsh` 0.2.2-rc.1 wrote a small feature in 95.4 seconds across 10 turns and 14 tool calls, produced two files, and the project's own tests passed 3 of 3.

What happened in the other two arms matters more than the arm that worked. Both refused to write anything in their non-interactive defaults, and both still exited 0. An exit code of zero means the process finished. It does not mean the work happened. Any CI job or nightly script that trusts the exit code alone is measuring the wrong thing, and this is the failure mode to test for on the first day.

We did not run the other two arms successfully, so this article makes no claim about their output quality.

## What to check before you pay
Five actions, none of which needs a subscription.

1. **Pick one real task from your own backlog**, small enough to finish in an hour, and run it in whichever harness you already have.
2. **Time it**, and count the turns and tool calls the harness reports. Those three numbers describe the run better than any leaderboard.
3. **Check whether the files landed**, not whether the process exited cleanly.
4. **Run it twice** with the same prompt. A harness that succeeds once and fails once is a different purchase.
5. **Before paying for a tier, ask what the processing fee is** in ringgit, and get it in writing.

There is no honest way to reproduce a leaderboard. What you can reproduce is your own row.

Take one task, run it in one harness, and write down the same five fields the boards print: the model, the agent, the settings, the score (did the tests pass), and the cost in tokens or ringgit. That is your benchmark, it is comparable to itself next month, and it does not depend on anyone's marketing page.

The one thing that will bite you is the exit code. A run that exits 0 without writing files looks like a pass in every log you have. Check the artefact, every time.

### Sources

- SWE-bench leaderboard, Verified tab — https://www.swebench.com/ (checked 2026-11-23)
- Terminal-bench 4.1 leaderboard — https://www.tbench.ai/ (checked 2026-11-23)
- Aider polyglot leaderboard — https://aider.chat/docs/leaderboards/ (checked 2026-11-23)
- CommandCode, pricing — https://commandcode.ai/pricing (checked 2026-11-23)
- OpenCode, Go subscription docs — https://opencode.ai/docs/console/go (checked 2026-11-23)
- DeepSeek, API pricing — https://api-docs.deepseek.com/quick_start/pricing (checked 2026-11-23)
- Hacker News, Show HN: Command Code GOAT (5 August 2026) — https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=49188656 (checked 2026-11-23)

## Google Business Profile: the fields that decide visibility

URL: https://upahje.my/en/articles/google-business-profile-fields
Checked: 2026-11-23

Google's own rules decide this, and they are specific. Your name must be the name customers use in the real world, you get one profile per business, and categories must describe the business rather than its keywords. Get those wrong and the profile can be restricted; get them right and the rest is filling documented fields.

## What does Google check first?

Four things, and they are all wording rules rather than technical settings.

| What Google documents | What it means for your profile |
| --- | --- |
| "Your name should reflect your business's real-world name, as used consistently on your storefront, website, stationery, and as known to customers." | No keyword stuffing in the name. "Kedai Kasut Ali" is a name; "Kedai Kasut Ali Murah KL Best" is a rule violation |
| "Use as few categories as possible to describe your overall core business from the provided list." | The category answers "this business IS a…", so it is a shoe shop, not "shoe shop near me with parking" |
| "Do not use categories solely as keywords or to describe attributes of your business." | Attributes have their own fields. Using categories for them is what leads to restrictions |
| "There should only be one profile per business, as this can cause problems with how your information displays on Google Maps and Search." | Two profiles for one shop, usually created by two people, is a documented problem rather than a growth tactic |

All four are quoted from Google's guidelines page, read 23 November 2026.

## What about the address, or no address at all?

A service-area business and a shopfront are different configurations, and Google documents both.

The location resource carries `address` and `serviceArea`, and a service-area business manages areas instead of a storefront. Google's own example is delivery-only brands working from shared kitchens, which "must hide their address and add service areas to that specific brand". If you deliver and do not have a walk-in counter, running a storefront profile is the mismatch to fix first.

## Which fields are worth filling this month?

Hours and the sub-resources Google documents, in the order they change a customer's decision.

1. **Regular hours** — `regularHours` on the location resource. Wrong hours generate the one-star review that says "closed when it says open".
2. **Special hours** — `specialHours`, for public holidays and the week you close for a family event. Malaysia has enough public holidays that leaving this empty guarantees at least one wrong visit.
3. **More hours** — `moreHours`, for departments or services inside the same premises, such as a workshop counter with different hours from the retail floor.
4. **Attributes** — managed as a sub-resource through `getAttributes` / `updateAttributes`. This is where "parking available" and "wheelchair accessible" belong, not in the category.
5. **Photos and media** — `accounts.locations.media`, with content governed by Google's prohibited-content policy.
6. **Posts** — `accounts.locations.localPosts`, useful for offers with an expiry rather than permanent information.
7. **Q&A** — `accounts.locations.questions` with `answers`, which is the field most businesses leave for strangers to fill.
8. **Review replies** — `accounts.locations.reviews`, the API surface for what customers actually read.

All of those are documented in Google's Business Profile API reference, read 23 November 2026. The API names matter even if you never write code: they are the fields the form on the website is editing.

## What gets a profile suspended, and what do you do?

Google documents both the suspension process and the appeal, and the appeal page contains the sentence to read before anything else.

A suspended profile is handled through "Fix suspended or disabled profiles", which asks for a spreadsheet of Business Profile IDs plus supporting documents such as business registration, licence or tax certificates, or utility bills. For content restrictions, the appeal page states: "If you haven't verified your Business Profile, content associated with your Business Profile might not appear across Google. Before you submit an appeal, check your verification status."

That sentence is the whole reason to keep verification current. An appeal filed before verification is resolved is an appeal that stalls.

## What could we not verify?

Google publishes nothing in these pages about how profiles are ranked in local search, so this article makes no claim about ranking factors beyond the documented fields. Several help-centre IDs returned "Sorry, this page can't be found" during the pass, so only the pages Google itself links, or that the scan surfaced, are cited. There is also no published figure for how long verification or an appeal takes.

## What to fix first
Five actions, none of which needs an agency.

1. **Read your own business name** against the real-world rule, and fix it in the profile rather than the listing on a directory.
2. **Check there is exactly one profile** for the business, including one someone created years ago and forgot.
3. **Decide storefront or service area**, and make the address and service areas match that decision.
4. **Fill regular and special hours** for the next two months of public holidays.
5. **Check your verification status** and keep the document that proves your business exists, because a suspension would ask for it.

The smallest version is an audit, not an integration: open your profile, and go field by field against Google's guidelines page, marking each one as documented-and-correct, documented-but-wrong, or empty.

You need the guidelines page, your own profile, and a spare hour. The cost is that some corrections trigger re-verification, so change the name and category last, once the rest is right, and do not change them again the same week.

[What an AI agent can and cannot do for a Malaysian SME](https://upahje.my/en/articles/what-an-ai-agent-can-do)

[More on buying automation](https://upahje.my/en/articles/category/buying-guides)

### Sources

- Google, guidelines for representing your business on Google — https://support.google.com/business/answer/3038177 (checked 2026-11-23)
- Google, service-area businesses — https://support.google.com/business/answer/3038163 (checked 2026-11-23)
- Google, fix suspended or disabled profiles — https://support.google.com/business/answer/4569145 (checked 2026-11-23)
- Google, appeal Business Profile content and profile restrictions — https://support.google.com/business/answer/13597551 (checked 2026-11-23)
- Google, Business Profile API reference (locations resource) — https://developers.google.com/my-business/reference/rest/v4/accounts.locations (checked 2026-11-23)

## What a leaderboard row actually measures

URL: https://upahje.my/en/articles/leaderboard-row-anatomy
Checked: 2026-11-23

Five things, and the score is only one of them: the model, the agent that drove it, the settings, the score, and the cost. Read the first two before the number. The Terminal-bench row for DeepSeek reads 38.5% ± 3.8% under Claude Code, with 8.2 billion tokens, which makes it a DeepSeek model's result inside someone else's harness.

## What is in a leaderboard row?

![A landscape diagram with columns for model, agent, settings, score and cost. The example row is DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 at max, run under Claude Code on Terminal-bench 4.1, scoring 38.5 percent plus or minus 3.8 with 8.2 billion tokens. A footer states that neither CommandCode nor OpenCode appears in the agent column](/figures/leaderboard-row-anatomy.svg)
*Read the agent column first: it decides whose number the score is.*

The Terminal-bench page prints its columns as RANK, MODEL, AGENT, RESOLUTION RATE, RELEASE DATE, TOKENS and COST. The DeepSeek row reads:

| Field | Value as printed |
| --- | --- |
| Model | DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 (max) |
| Agent | Claude Code |
| Resolution rate | 38.5% ± 3.8% |
| Tokens | 8.2B |
| Release date | Oct 17, 2026 |

Change the agent and the number changes, which is why the column exists.

## Which names appear on the boards at all

SWE-bench Verified's agent column lists only mini-SWE-agent. Terminal-bench 4.1 lists Claude Code, Codex, Antigravity CLI, GitHub Copilot, Grok Build and mini-SWE-agent. Neither board has CommandCode or OpenCode in the agent column.

The model names are a separate question, and thinner than the marketing suggests. SWE-bench Verified has DeepSeek V3.2 (high) at 70.00% resolved with an average cost of $0.45, and DeepSeek V3.2 Reasoner at 60.00% with an average cost of $0.03, both under mini-SWE-agent. SWE-bench has no entry for DeepSeek V4.1 Flash or V4 Pro: an absence on the board, not a bad score. Aider polyglot's newest visible run directory is dated 23 August 2025 and its top row is gpt-5 (high) at 88.0% for $29.08, which is not a current reading.

## What the comparison published, and what the run records

The archived page, snapshot 25 October 2026, lists three interactive demos for Round 1: DeepSeek Platform, OpenCode Go and CommandCode GOAT, each a demo path under a vivarium conceit. The catalog is the evidence: each entry carries a title, a description, a path and a tone, and no score, duration, token count or cost. The demos themselves live in `nazzysar/deepseek-benchmarks`, and their SHA-256 hashes match that repository's `rounds/checksums.json`; scanned for text, they carry in-game numbers only, with no build time, token count, cost or score caption.

The GOAT arm's own session records are more informative than its demo. Three redacted transcripts in `nazzysar/commandcode-goat-ecosystem-sess` carry 1,123, 582 and 1,091 records. The lead session retried 33 times: 23 SERVER, 10 TRANSPORT, 0 TIMEOUT; across the three, 94 retries split 57 / 37 / 0. Five turns lasted 7,565.5 s, 2,636.0 s, 150.5 s, 117.6 s and 3.9 s, totalling 10,473.5 s, about 2 h 55 m. The run made 161 tool calls, 140 steps, 138 assistant messages and 25 user messages, on `deepseek/deepseek-v4.1-flash` through provider `commandcode-goat`.

That is a reliability profile, and it says nothing about output quality. There are no token counts and no cost fields in those records, and the site's data model has no cost field, so no cost comparison can be built from them.

- SWE-bench leaderboard, Verified tab — https://www.swebench.com/ (checked 2026-11-23)
- Terminal-bench 4.1 leaderboard — https://www.tbench.ai/ (checked 2026-11-23)

## Don't rewrite your site. Rewrite the 5%.

URL: https://upahje.my/en/articles/rewrite-the-five-percent
Checked: 2026-11-23

Two repositories published five days apart carry 11,986 stars between them as of 24 November 2026, and give opposite advice. One says port the whole app to Rust, piece by piece. The other says port only the 5% that is slow. Both are MIT, and both are right. What decides which one you need is not your stack.

## Two MIT repos, five days apart, argue opposite fixes

`rust-anything`, created 16 November 2026, has 8,782 stars as of 24 November 2026. Its description promises the whole application: rewrite it in Rust one piece at a time, checked against the original's recorded behaviour at every step. Its README claims one port: Prettier, "19x faster", with "15,861 of 17,224 recorded runs" in Rust and every run byte-identical.

`fast-anything`, created 21 November 2026, has 3,204 stars as of 24 November 2026. Its description argues against that scope: don't rewrite it in Rust, rewrite the 5% that's slow, port the hot functions, prove they behave the same.

They disagree about scope, and money follows scope.

## One ports the whole app; the other ports one function

`rust-anything` records what your app does, your agent writes the replacement piece by piece, and each piece is checked against the recording before the next.

`fast-anything` profiles the app, ranks functions by time and portability, records up to 500 real calls of the function it picks, derives edge cases, and replays them. Nothing is enabled until every case matches, floats to within 1e-9, errors where the original errors. Its recorder caps at 500 calls; the README shows a wrong port caught by "148 of 500" recorded calls.

Neither repo was executed for this article. The figures are theirs; the mechanisms show in their source.

## The test is whether the slowness is one function or every request

One question decides the camp, and it is not app size.

If ten requests pass through one function, you have a 5% problem in a whole-app costume. Profile it, port that function, prove equivalence, ship. The rest of the app stays put, so the blast radius is one function and the rollback is a flag.

If every part is uniformly mediocre, there is no single hot function; there are forty, each slow by the same margin. That is a rewrite problem, and one function moves the number by almost nothing.

| Your symptom | The camp that fits | What it publishes as evidence | What goes wrong if you pick wrong |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| One endpoint, one script, one image transform dominates the runtime | fast-anything | 500 recorded calls replayed per port; 148 of 500 caught one wrong port | Nothing, if the function is pure. If it touches I/O, it will refuse and you have lost a day |
| The same code path appears in every request | fast-anything, applied twice | Same 500-call verification, per function | You fix the first hotspot and the second appears; two ports, not one |
| Every screen feels slow, no single hotspot | rust-anything | 15,861 of 17,224 recorded runs in Rust, every run byte-identical | Months of porting, a compile step in the loop, and a rewrite still half done |
| The slow part is a query or an unoptimised asset | neither | — | You port code around a database problem and the database stays slow |

The last row is the common mistake: a 4-second page can be one uncompressed hero image, and no amount of Rust will touch it.

## For an SME site, the answer is the 5%

For a Malaysian small-business site, the slow thing is almost always one image, one query, or one blocking script, and the correct response is to fix that and stop. A full port is a decision for a team with a profiling budget and a release process. For a shop with five pages and a product list, an eleven-thousand-star framework is not the constraint.

Before you accept a quote to rebuild, ask which function or query is slow and what number it produces. A developer who cannot name it is quoting a rewrite, and a rewrite has no end date.

## Measure three things before you believe either camp

Three numbers, any one of which can end the project.

1. **Largest contentful paint** for your product page on a throttled 4G profile. If the image is the element, the fix is an image, not a language.
2. **The slowest query in your database log** for a normal week. If one query is seconds and the rest milliseconds, you have found the 5%.
3. **The largest asset the page downloads**, by byte size. A 2 MB image on a five-page site is a five-minute fix that beats a rewrite.

They cost nothing, take an evening, and give you the vocabulary to reject the expensive answer.

## A rewrite has no end date; a five-percent port does

A whole-app port ends when the last module is checked, a date nobody can promise. A single-function port ends when the recorded calls match: a condition, not a schedule.

If your slowness is one function, take the small port. If it is everywhere, price the rewrite honestly, months included. The expensive mistake is buying the big fix for the small problem.

## Where the same data gets typed three times

URL: https://upahje.my/en/articles/same-data-typed-three-times
Checked: 2026-11-23

Adoption is not the problem. In 2024, 97.2% of Malaysian establishments reported using computers, 95.3% had internet access, and 74.4% had a web presence. The duplication happens one layer back: a customer-facing system that was digitised, and a back office that was not. The same order then exists in two places, and a person reconciles it.

## What do the official numbers say?

Three figures from DOSM's ICT and e-commerce release for establishments, data year 2024, published 2025. They measure adoption, and they measure it well.

| Measure | 2024 | Change from the previous year |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Establishments using computers | 97.2% | up 0.6 percentage points from 96.6% |
| Establishments with internet access | 95.3% | up from 94.0% |
| Establishments with a web presence | 74.4% | up from 72.7% |

Read them together and the picture is a business that already has a computer, a connection and often a website. What the release does not measure is how many separate systems those establishments run, or how much time goes into moving data between them. That absence matters, and it is the reason this article avoids a number for "hours lost".

## What does the research say about how it is used?

Khazanah Research Institute, with MDEC, published a finding in May 2026 that describes the pattern without counting it, so it is worth quoting rather than paraphrasing: digital tools "are often implemented in isolation and used reactively, driven by immediate operational needs rather than longer-term strategic planning".

The same paper describes "fragmented systems where customer-facing functions are digitised while back-end processes remain manual", and adds that technology use is "typically confined to basic infrastructure and standalone applications, with minimal use of analytics, automation, or enterprise systems". It also names the precursor: "many MSMEs operate with limited documentation, weak record-keeping, and constrained access to financing".

This is a think-tank finding, dated 25 May 2026, not a statistic. It says the shape of the problem, and it is careful not to put a number on it.

## Where does a single order get typed three times?

Follow one order. It arrives as a message, gets written into a quotation, becomes an invoice, and then a delivery order or a job sheet. Each of those documents exists in a system, and in most small businesses the systems do not talk.

The quotation lives in a template. The invoice is issued through accounting software. The delivery order is a form someone prints, or a note in a chat. The stock count is a spreadsheet that one person maintains. Four records of one event, and the only integration is a person remembering which one is current.

That is not a technology failure at the level DOSM measures. Every one of those tools is software. It is a fragmentation failure, exactly the pattern KRI describes, and it costs a business in rework rather than in licences.

## Why does e-Invoice force the point?

Because LHDN now checks the document, not the intent, and the check happens at issuance.

Three rules make that concrete, all from LHDN's own validation documentation and guidelines:

1. **Duplicates are checked.** The Duplicate Document Validator looks for documents submitted recently that are similar or identical, so a second submission of the same invoice is not invisible.
2. **The taxpayer must be valid on the date of issuance.** The Taxpayer Validator checks that the taxpayers referenced are valid at that date, not at the date someone corrected the record.
3. **Corrections are time-boxed.** A buyer may reject and a seller may cancel within 72 hours of validation. After that, the only correction is a new e-Invoice in the form of a credit, debit or refund note.

So the invoice data has to be right once, at the source, before an automated system touches it. An automation that copies a wrong supplier code into a submitted invoice does not create a small error; it creates a correction document with its own tax treatment. We covered the filing timeline in [what e-Invoice automation covers](https://upahje.my/en/articles/what-einvoice-automation-covers); this article is about why the data behind it has to be single.

## What does nobody publish?

Three gaps, and they are worth naming because they are the numbers every vendor deck uses.

No published figure gives the number of software systems a typical Malaysian SME runs. DOSM's release covers computers, internet and web presence; there is no application-count question in it.

No published Malaysian figure gives the ringgit cost of duplicated entry or of integration. Vendor pages assert savings without a baseline, which makes the percentage meaningless.

And the two famous "hours lost" numbers are not Malaysian. One is a vendor case study claiming "around 60%" of admin hours removed; another is a vendor case study claiming "20 hours of weekly manual work" cut. The widely repeated "12-16 hours per week" traces to an unsigned blog citing US labour-statistics and consultancy data, which is not a Malaysian measurement and should not be printed as one.

## The checklist you will see quoted

Written process, named owner, clean data source, exception path. That four-part framing is a Malaysian operations consultancy's article, published on its own site with no byline, written about the KRI/MDEC paper. It is a vendor's checklist, not an official one, and no government body publishes those four as a standard. Useful as a way to think; not citable as policy.

## What to map this week
Five actions, none of which needs a purchase.

1. **Pick one document** you issue often: a quotation, an invoice, a delivery order.
2. **Follow it end to end**, and write down every place a person retypes something that already existed.
3. **Count the copies** of that one record, and name who owns which copy.
4. **Find the field that gets fixed by hand** most often, because that is where the source is wrong.
5. **Write the exception path** for the one case that happens weekly: what should the system say, and who decides.

Start with a one-page map rather than a system: a spreadsheet with one row per step of the document, and columns for system, owner, and where the data is retyped.

You need the document, the person who handles it, and an hour. The cost is that the map will show steps nobody admitted to, including the WhatsApp message that is currently the integration. Write it down anyway; the message is the real process, and automating around it without knowing it is how a project fails.

### Sources

- DOSM, usage of ICT and e-commerce by establishment, 2025 release (data year 2024) — https://www.dosm.gov.my/portal-main/release-content/usage-of-ict-and-e-commerce-by-establishment2025 (checked 2026-11-23)
- Khazanah Research Institute with MDEC, from survival to scale (25 May 2026) — https://www.krinstitute.org/press-release/from-survival-to-scale-digitalisation-among-malaysias-micro-and-small-enterprises-remains-broad-but-shallow (checked 2026-11-23)
- LHDN, MyInvois SDK document validation rules — https://sdk.myinvois.hasil.gov.my/document-validation-rules/ (checked 2026-11-23)

- Friction, Malaysia SME digitalisation note (vendor article, no byline) — https://friction.com.my/insights/malaysia-sme-digitalisation-from-survival-to-scale-2026 (checked 2026-11-23)

## What an AI agent can and cannot do for a small business

URL: https://upahje.my/en/articles/what-an-ai-agent-can-do
Checked: 2026-11-23

An AI agent runs a loop by itself: it reads a task, calls tools, looks at the result and decides the next step until the job is done. That covers repetitive work with a clear finish line. It does not cover judgement, money it is not authorised to move, or anything a customer would need explained to them by a person.

## What is an agent, as opposed to a chatbot?

A chatbot answers. An agent answers, then does something about it, which is why it needs tools it can call (a tool is one thing it is allowed to do, such as look up an order or send an email), a loop that continues after a tool returns, and a transcript, meaning a written record of what it did.

Anthropic's own wording for the layer that runs this is an agent harness, which is the program that holds the conversation and runs the tools, defined as "runs the agent loop, with sessions in an Anthropic-managed cloud sandbox or a self-hosted sandbox on your own infrastructure" ([Claude Code docs, read 23 Nov 2026](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/overview)). Two consequences follow for a small business: the agent can touch real systems, and the harness, not the model, decides what it is allowed to touch.

## What can it do unattended?

![Three panels: work that runs unattended such as sorting an inbox; work the agent prepares for a human to approve such as refunds and customer messages; work that is not for an agent such as judgement calls and physical tasks](/figures/what-an-ai-agent-can-do.svg)
*Sort the work before you choose a tool: unattended, prepared, and not agent work.*

Unattended work is work where a wrong answer is cheap to spot and cheap to undo.

| What it does on its own | Why it qualifies |
| --- | --- |
| Read an inbox and sort messages into buckets | A misfiled email is visible and reversible |
| Extract fields from an invoice or delivery order and enter them | The source document stays available for comparison |
| Copy data between two systems on a schedule | A failed copy can be re-run |
| Draft replies, reports or summaries for someone to send | A person still presses send |
| Watch a queue and alert a human when a threshold trips | The agent escalates rather than acts |

## What needs a human before it happens?

Approval work is work where the cost of a wrong action is not recoverable by re-running it.

| Needs a human | Why |
| --- | --- |
| Anything that moves money: refunds, payments, waivers | A wrong transfer is not undone by an apology |
| Sending a message to a customer on your behalf | Tone and commitment are business decisions |
| Deleting or overwriting a record | There is nothing to restore from |
| Changing prices, stock levels or availability | A wrong price is honoured, not corrected |
| Anything legal or regulatory: e-Invoice submissions, contracts, filings | The liability sits with the business, not the agent |

So let the agent prepare and let a person approve. An agent that drafts a refund and waits for a click saves the typing and takes none of the risk. I would not run one any other way, and the vendor demos that skip the approval step are the ones to be suspicious of.

## What can it not do at all?

Four categories, and no amount of prompting changes them.

1. **Judgement calls with no rule to follow.** Whether a complaint is fair, whether a supplier is trustworthy, whether to keep a client. An agent can gather the facts; the decision is not a fact.
2. **Anything physical.** Deliveries, installations, inspections. A WhatsApp bot can book a technician; it cannot change a part.
3. **Knowledge it does not have.** An agent answers from what it can reach. If your stock is in someone's head, the agent will be confidently wrong.
4. **Guaranteed accuracy.** Every agent produces a plausible wrong answer sometimes. That is why the approval column exists.

## What does it cost in ringgit?

Two bills. The smaller one gets the attention.

**Running it.** Token rates are published, so this is arithmetic rather than a guess. At 2,000 input and 500 output tokens per task, Claude Haiku 5.5 costs `0.002 million × USD 0.10 = USD 0.0002` for input plus `0.0005 million × USD 0.50 = USD 0.00025` for output, which is USD 0.00045 a task. At the Bank Negara middle rate of **4.1145** (read 19 November 2026), that is about RM0.00185. A thousand tasks a month is **RM1.85**. A teh tarik at a mamak is RM2 to RM3, which is our own comparison, not a published index.

**Building it.** Malaysian publishers quote project prices for automation work: **RM400** for a simple process build ([Pang Jun Han, read 23 Nov 2026](https://pangjunhan.vercel.app/ai-automation)) and **RM6,000-plus** for autonomous task execution ([Autoflow Solutions, read 23 Nov 2026](https://www.autoflow-solutions.com/my/services)). A starter workflow build from a studio starts at **RM1,500** ([KodeSME, read 23 Nov 2026](https://kodesme.klyihao.com/)).

So the build is hundreds to thousands of ringgit and the running cost is a few ringgit. If a supplier quotes a large monthly token bill for a small workflow, ask them to show the arithmetic against the published rate; ours takes three lines. What the rate cards do not state is the monthly support fee after launch, so ask for it before you compare quotes.

## Where to start this week
Five actions, none of which needs a purchase or a developer.

1. **Write down the one task you would automate first**, and what "done" looks like for it, in one sentence.
2. **Count how often it happens** for a week, on paper. Under five times a day, the case is weak.
3. **List the systems it touches** and whether the agent would only read from them or also write.
4. **Find the failure that would hurt**, and decide whether a person should approve before it happens.
5. **Ask two suppliers the six checks below**, and compare the answers rather than the prices.

Begin with a script that reads a CSV of support emails, calls one model per row, and writes a draft reply into a second CSV. It is not an agent yet. That is deliberate, because it proves the loop before you add tools.

- **What it needs:** a file of sample rows, an API key (a string that identifies your account to the model provider), and about 20 lines of Python. No server.
- **What it costs:** at 2,000 input and 500 output tokens per row, about **RM0.00185 a row**, so a hundred rows is under 20 sen.
- **Where it breaks first:** a model reading a CSV column will happily mis-parse an empty cell and invent a customer name. Log every input row beside its output, or you will debug the wrong half.

## How do I tell a demo from something that keeps running?

A demo works once, in front of you. Something that keeps running survives a bad day. Six checks. Each answer should be a thing someone can show you.

1. **Show me the transcript.** A working agent records what it did, step by step. If there is no log, there is no evidence it ran.
2. **What happens when a step fails?** Retry, queue or alert. Silence is not an answer.
3. **What is it allowed to touch?** The list of systems, read or write, should be short enough to say aloud.
4. **Who owns the keys and the accounts?** Yours, in your account, revocable.
5. **What happens when the vendor changes something?** Ask who fixes it and at what price.
6. **Who is watching it next month?** An agent with no owner stops being maintained the week after the invoice is paid.

## The e-Invoice threshold is now RM3 million

URL: https://upahje.my/en/articles/what-einvoice-automation-covers
Checked: 2026-11-23

The line moved on 1 September 2026: from RM1 million to RM3 million of annual revenue or sales. LHDN's own statement says businesses below it are not required to implement e-Invoice, and puts the number of traders who benefit at more than 1.1 million. Above the line, the programme has been running since 1 August 2024 and has already logged 265,379 taxpayers and more than 1.84 billion e-Invoices.

## The exemption is written in the statement, not implied

The rule is a sentence, not a calculation. The statement reads: "PMKS dengan pendapatan atau jualan tahunan kurang daripada RM3 juta tidak diwajibkan untuk melaksanakan e-Invois", which is MSMEs with annual revenue or sales below RM3 million are not required to implement e-Invoice.

Three things follow from that sentence, and only three.

1. The number is **RM3 million**, not the RM1 million that applied before 1 September 2026.
2. It measures **annual revenue or sales**, not profit, headcount or registered capital.
3. It says **not required**. It does not say prohibited, and the same statement encourages voluntary participation.

The Prime Minister announced the change in the 2026 National Day address, and LHDN published the statement on 30 August 2026, one day before it took effect.

A business with RM2.9 million in annual sales sits below the line, so e-Invoice is not required; the test is the annual figure, not a single good quarter.

## The programme numbers are already large

These are LHDN's own totals, not a projection.

| What the statement reports | Figure |
| --- | --- |
| New exemption threshold, from 1 September 2026 | RM3 million |
| Threshold it replaced | RM1 million |
| Traders covered by the exemption | more than 1.1 million |
| Taxpayers in the programme since 1 August 2024 | 265,379 |
| e-Invoices issued since 1 August 2024 | more than 1.84 billion |

Read the last two rows as adoption, not compliance. A taxpayer can be registered and issue a modest number of documents, and the totals say nothing about how many businesses are fully compliant.

## What the system checks at issuance

For anyone above the threshold, the submission is checked by eight validators before it is accepted: structure (UBL 2.1 for invoices), core fields, signature, taxpayer validity, referenced documents, codes, duplicates and currency. The duplicate check looks for documents submitted recently that are similar or identical, and the taxpayer check tests validity at the date of issuance.

That matters for data quality rather than for software choice. If the invoice data is wrong at the moment of issuance, the validation catches it, and the correction path is not an edit. A buyer may reject and a seller may cancel within 72 hours of validation; after that, a correction requires a new e-Invoice in the form of a credit, debit or refund note.

## The penalty is cited, and the amount is not published

LHDN cites Section 120 of the Income Tax Act 1967. No ringgit figure appears in the statement, and none was found on the pages checked. A business deciding how much to spend on compliance should treat that as an unknown rather than as a small risk.

## If you are under RM3 million, wait for a customer to ask

A business below the threshold should not adopt e-Invoice for its own sake. The requirement is lifted, voluntary participation is encouraged but not rewarded, and the operational cost is real. Adopt it when a large customer or a government buyer requires it, and then handle that customer's transactions rather than converting every invoice you issue.

The exception is a business planning to cross RM3 million. If revenue is close to the line, running one quarter of e-Invoice in parallel is cheaper than discovering the obligation in the quarter it applies.

## What could not be verified

Four claims that circulate in guidance and commentary are not in the statement, and none was confirmed from a primary page.

The group-ownership rule, reported as disqualifying a sub-RM3 million business that belongs to a larger group, is cited to a guideline paragraph that was not opened.

The RM50,000 annual deduction for voluntary adoption, mentioned in commentary for years of assessment 2024 to 2027, appears only in secondary sources.

Whether a business that started under the old RM1 million line may stop is not answered in the statement. The guidance is silent on the reverse case.

And the per-phase relaxation dates sit in a graphic in the guideline PDF rather than in its text, so they are not reproduced here.

- LHDN media statement HASiL/2026/08/30-44, AMBANG PENGECUALIAN PELAKSANAAN E-INVOIS DINAIKKAN — https://www.hasil.gov.my/wp-content/uploads/20260830-Kenyataan-Media-HASiL_AMBANG-PENGECUALIAN-E_INVOIS-DINAIKKAN.pdf (checked 2026-11-23)
- LHDN, e-Invois programme page — https://www.hasil.gov.my/e-invois (checked 2026-11-23)
- MyInvois SDK, document validation rules — https://sdk.myinvois.hasil.gov.my/document-validation-rules/ (checked 2026-11-23)
- LHDN, Garis Panduan e-Invois Versi 4.8 — https://www.hasil.gov.my/wp-content/uploads/Garis-Panduan-e-Invois-LHDNM.pdf (checked 2026-11-23)

## What a WhatsApp chatbot costs, per message

URL: https://upahje.my/en/articles/whatsapp-chatbot-costs-malaysia
Checked: 2026-11-24

A WhatsApp bot in Malaysia costs nothing up to 1,000 service messages a month per business phone number, and nothing at all for messages a customer sends you. Past that allowance, a marketing template is RM0.3467, utility, authentication and service are RM0.0564 each, and a Malaysian vendor adds RM200 to RM1,500 a month to run the bot.

## What is free and what is billed

Three different bills arrive at a WhatsApp bot, and they come from two different companies. Meta's card covers the per-message charges; your vendor's invoice covers everything else.

| What | Status | Who bills it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| The WhatsApp Business app | Free | Nobody |
| Messages a customer sends you | Never charged | Nobody |
| The first 1,000 service messages per number per calendar month | Free, no rollover | Nobody |
| Any message inside the open 24-hour window | Free | Nobody |
| Marketing templates | RM0.3467 each | Meta |
| Authentication templates | RM0.0564 each | Meta |
| Utility templates outside the window | RM0.0564 each | Meta |
| Service messages past the 1,000 allowance | RM0.0564 each | Meta |
| Meta Business Agent messages | Billed per million tokens | Meta |
| BSP markup, hosting and seats | The vendor's own fee | Your vendor |

The allowance is per business phone number and resets each calendar month; unused messages do not carry over. Service messages past it have been charged since 1 October 2026.

Utility, authentication and service are RM0.0564, and the first 1,000 service messages per number per month are free.

## Meta bills per delivered message, by category

Per message, per category, and only when the message is delivered. The unit is not a conversation and not a session.

Three rules from Meta's pricing page set the bill, all effective from 1 October 2026 for the rate card used here:

1. **Charged on delivery only.** "Businesses are only charged when a message is delivered. Meta does not charge for messages sent."
2. **One direction only.** Business-to-user messages are charged; messages from users to the business are not.
3. **One category per message.** A message has one of five categories, so it can incur at most one charge.

The five categories are marketing, utility, authentication, service, and Meta Business Agent, which Meta introduced on 1 July 2026 and prices in tokens rather than per message.

## A marketing template costs RM0.3467

These are the published MYR prices, not conversions. Meta publishes a separate card for each currency, and the Malaysian buyer should quote the MYR one.

| Category | Price per delivered message (MYR) | Price on the USD card | What it is for |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Marketing | 0.3467 | 0.086 | Promotions, re-engagement, offers |
| Utility | 0.0564 | 0.014 | Order updates, receipts, appointment reminders |
| Authentication | 0.0564 | 0.014 | One-time passcodes |
| Authentication, international | 0.1685 | 0.0418 | Passcodes delivered outside the domestic route |
| Service | 0.0564 | 0.014 | Replies inside the customer service window |

The MYR and USD cards move together at about 4.03, but the MYR figure is the one Meta publishes for Malaysia, so no exchange rate is applied in this article. Both cards carry the same effective date: 1 October 2026.

## The 24-hour window decides which rate applies

![A left-to-right diagram: a customer message opens a 24-hour window; a reply inside it is a service message at RM0.0564 with the first 1,000 per number per month free; a message after the window closes must be a template, at RM0.3467 for marketing or RM0.0564 for utility and authentication](/figures/whatsapp-chatbot-costs-malaysia.svg)
*The clock, not the message text, decides which rate applies.*

Because a free-form reply is only allowed inside it, and outside it you must use a paid template.

The customer service window opens and resets with each user message, and lasts 24 hours. Inside it, a business may send non-template messages, which are service messages. Outside it, the only way to start a conversation is a template, which falls into marketing, utility or authentication.

The practical shape: a customer asks a question, you answer inside 24 hours as a service message, and that answer sits inside the free tier for the first 1,000 a month. If you follow up three days later with a promotion, that is a marketing template at RM0.3467 per delivered message.

## Why the two Meta pages look like they disagree

The WhatsApp Business marketing site says "we do not charge for service messages, or for utility messages businesses send in response to users". Meta's developer pricing page prices service at RM0.0564 with the first 1,000 free.

There is no contradiction once the allowance and the clock are applied. A reply to a customer sits inside the open 24-hour window, where nothing is charged, and the first 1,000 service messages each month are free on top of that. The marketing page is describing the common case; the developer page is describing the tariff behind it. A business only meets the RM0.0564 service rate after 1,000 service messages in a month.

One genuine difference remains. Meta's documentation says a free entry point window "may remain open for up to 7 days", while the marketing site says "for the following 3 days (72 hours), all of your messages are not charged". Plan on 3 days, because that is the shorter promise and the only one a business can rely on without overestimating free volume.

## A local vendor bills a platform fee on top of Meta

Three publishers, three shapes. These are build-and-subscription prices, not message rates, and Meta bills its messages separately.

| Publisher | What is published | Price | Unit |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| AIRS | AI agent on the business's own WhatsApp number, no setup fee for standard onboarding | from RM599 | per month, per outlet |
| The Crunch | Self-serve route | up to RM999 | per month; built systems quoted on scope |
| AlwaysON | Total cost of a chatbot for a Malaysian small business | RM200 to RM1,500 | per month, total range |

AIRS also states the market band as RM300 to RM3,000-plus per month, and AlwaysON notes that platform fees are "only 40-60% of the total cost", which is a useful warning: the subscription is not the whole bill.

## What to count before you sign
Five actions, none of which needs a purchase.

1. **Export last month's outbound WhatsApp messages** and tag each one marketing, utility, authentication or service.
2. **Count the service messages** and compare against 1,000 per number. If you are under it, most of your bill may be zero.
3. **Find the messages you send outside the 24-hour window.** Those are the marketing templates at RM0.3467 each, and they dominate small bills.
4. **Multiply the marketing count by 0.3467** and the paid service count by 0.0564, and compare that total with RM200 to RM1,500 of vendor fees.
5. **Ask each vendor whether their price includes Meta's message charges**, and get the answer in writing, because the two bills come from different companies.

Before talking to a vendor, price your own last month from the published card with a script, so you know the volume before you talk to a vendor.

- **What it needs:** a CSV of your outbound messages with a category column, and a spreadsheet or 15 lines of Python that multiplies counts by 0.3467 and 0.0564. No Meta account.
- **What it costs:** nothing, and it answers the only question that matters, which is whether your volume is a rounding error or a real monthly cost.
- **The one thing that will bite you:** counting messages you *sent* rather than messages *delivered*, and counting user-to-business messages, which Meta does not charge at all.

There is no honest free sandbox path documented in the pages read for this article, so this block stops at pricing your own data rather than inventing a test setup.

## What we could not verify

The dedicated international-authentication page was not opened, so that row rests on the Malaysia card alone. Utility and authentication volume tiers exist, but the tier files were not parsed, so any figure above list price is absent. Meta Business Agent is priced per million tokens with no Malaysia-specific per-message figure published, so no per-interaction cost is claimed. Only one of the three Malaysian vendors publishes a from-price with no setup fee; the other two quote on scope, so no market-wide build fee can be stated.

- Meta, WhatsApp pricing (per-message billing, 24-hour window, free tier, FEP) — https://developers.facebook.com/documentation/business-messaging/whatsapp/pricing (checked 2026-11-24)
- Meta, MYR list rates for Malaysia linked from the pricing page, effective 1 October 2026 — https://developers.facebook.com/documentation/business-messaging/whatsapp/pricing (checked 2026-11-24)
- WhatsApp Business, platform pricing (the free-service and 3-day FEP claims) — https://whatsappbusiness.com/products/platform-pricing/ (checked 2026-11-23)
- AIRS, WhatsApp AI chatbot price — https://airs.my/answers/whatsapp-ai-chatbot-malaysia-price (checked 2026-11-23)
- The Crunch, WhatsApp chatbot Malaysia — https://thecrunch.io/whatsapp-chatbot-malaysia/ (checked 2026-11-23)
- AlwaysON, WhatsApp chatbot pricing — https://alwayson.my/blog/whatsapp-chatbot-pricing (checked 2026-11-23)

## Your first automation should not be your worst process

URL: https://upahje.my/en/articles/your-first-automation-wrong-process
Checked: 2026-11-23

*This is an opinion piece. It argues a position from what we have seen reading and running these systems; it does not report a measurement.*

Most Malaysian SMEs automate the wrong process first. Not because they pick badly on price, but because they pick the process that annoys the owner most, and that process is usually the one nobody has ever written down. Automating it buries the mess under a tool instead of fixing it.

## Why is the worst process the wrong starting point?

Because the thing that makes a process painful is almost never the typing. It is the exceptions.

Take the invoice chase every small business has: a supplier sends the wrong quantity, the delivery order and the invoice disagree, someone calls to confirm, and the call produces a note in someone's WhatsApp. The typing is trivial. The knowledge of what to do when the numbers disagree is the whole job, and it lives in one person's head. Automate the typing and you have automated the cheap part while the expensive part gets quieter and harder to find.

## Argument one: automation removes the evidence

A manual process leaves a trail. Emails, scribbles, a correction someone made at 4pm on a Friday. Ugly, but readable, and it tells you where the exceptions were.

An automated process leaves a log, and the log only contains what you thought to log. When the first wrong invoice goes through, the investigation starts from what the tool recorded, which is usually the fields it knew about. The exception lives outside that.

There is a workable version of this: log the manual process for two weeks before touching it. A sheet with one row per instance, the time it took, and a column for what went wrong. That sheet is worth more than any automation quote, and it costs nothing. The [rates article](https://upahje.my/en/articles/automation-rates-malaysia-published) assumes you know your volume before you ask for a price; this is how you find out.

## Argument two: the first automation is a test, not a fix

The first one teaches your team how to buy, brief, test and maintain automation. Those are four separate skills, and a painful process is the worst training ground for them because failure is expensive and the person who understands it has no spare time.

Start with something boring. A weekly export that a junior copies between two systems. If it goes wrong, nobody's month is ruined, and you learn what a failed run looks like in your own logs. The [piece on telling a demo from something that keeps running](https://upahje.my/en/articles/what-an-ai-agent-can-do) is easier to apply when the stakes are low.

## Argument three: the worst process is often the wrong process

Pain is a signal that the process has accumulated exceptions, and exceptions usually mean the process is compensating for something upstream. The invoice mismatch is not an invoicing problem. It is a receiving problem, or a supplier problem, or a quoting problem.

Automating a compensating process locks the compensation in. Now you have a tool-shaped reason not to fix the thing that caused it. The argument is sometimes made in reverse, as "automate first, fix later", and it only works if the thing you automate is the source rather than the symptom.

## What should you do instead?

Three steps, and none of them needs a purchase.

1. **Write the process down**, in the order it happens, including the parts that are not steps: "ask Aminah because she knows the supplier".
2. **Track two weeks of it**, one row per instance, with a column for what went wrong. Two weeks is enough to see the shape.
3. **Pick the second most annoying process**, not the first. By then you know what a good brief looks like, and the process you avoid is the one with the most hidden exceptions.

If you want the sharper version: instrument, don't automate, until the exceptions are written down. Then automate the thing with a clear finish line and a cheap mistake, which is usually the boring process nobody complains about.

## Where I could be wrong

If the process is high volume, low variation and genuinely a copy-paste job, automating it first is fine, and waiting for two weeks of data is a waste of time. The argument here is about the process that generates complaints, not the one that generates rows.

And there is a real cost to waiting. Two weeks of tracking is two weeks of the pain continuing, and for some businesses that is not affordable. That trade is between knowing more and suffering longer, and only the owner can price it.

**Read next**

[What automation work costs in Malaysia, from published rates](https://upahje.my/en/articles/automation-rates-malaysia-published)

[More on buying automation](https://upahje.my/en/articles/category/buying-guides)

## Agent harness, AI harness, agent framework: what they mean

URL: https://upahje.my/en/articles/agent-harness-vs-ai-harness
Checked: 2026-11-19

An agent harness is the runtime that runs a model's agent loop: it holds the system prompt, executes tool calls, manages context, applies permissions and supplies a working environment. Vendors use "agent harness" or just "harness". "AI harness" is not a phrase the official sources I opened use, and "agent framework" is a different thing again.

## Who actually says "harness"?

Anthropic says "hosted agent harness", and the DeepSeek Harness package uses the bare word as its product noun.

Anthropic's own definition is the clearest: a hosted agent harness "runs the agent loop, with sessions in an Anthropic-managed cloud sandbox or a self-hosted sandbox on your own infrastructure" ([Claude Code docs, read 19 Nov 2026](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/overview)). The installed DeepSeek Harness package uses the word the same way, as in "Harness home" for its config directory ([package README, read 19 Nov 2026](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@deepseek-ai/dsh)). Neither treats it as a metaphor.

## What does the term imply, in practice?

Four things, and each one is a line rather than a walkthrough.

1. **Tool execution.** The harness runs the tool, not the model. The model chooses a tool and arguments, and the harness performs the call.
2. **A turn and step loop.** One message becomes a turn; the turn contains steps; each step is another exchange with the model when a tool result needs to go back.
3. **A transcript on disk.** The conversation is written to a file you can read: in this harness, compressed JSON Lines under `.dsh/sessions`.
4. **Permissions and approvals.** A harness decides what a tool is allowed to do, and records the policy. Without that, it is a chat client with extra steps.

How it walks through one message, step by step, is covered in [what an agent harness does with your request](https://upahje.my/en/articles/using-the-harness). This article is about the vocabulary, not the loop.

## Where does "AI harness" come from?

Not from the vendors I could read. Across the four official sources opened for this article, the phrase "AI harness" does not appear.

The method has a limit and I will state it: a search-engine query for the exact phrase returned a bot-check page instead of results, so I cannot claim no page anywhere uses it. What I can say is narrower and still useful: Anthropic says "agent harness", DeepSeek Harness says "harness", and neither uses "AI harness" on the pages I opened. When a blog uses "AI harness", it is borrowing the vendor word and adding a modifier that the vendors do not use.

| Term | Who uses it | What it means in that context |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Harness | DeepSeek Harness, Anthropic | The runtime that runs the agent loop and owns the environment |
| Agent harness | Anthropic, most vendor docs | The same runtime with the agent parts named: sessions, subagents, tool routing, approvals |
| AI harness | Marketing pages and blogs | No fixed meaning; on the sources read here, not a vendor term at all |
| Agent framework | Library authors | A code library for building agents, not a runtime that runs one |
| Agent workspace | OpenBot, MausBot | The product's own word for a harness plus a desktop or a machine per bot |

## Why does the distinction matter when buying?

Because the words describe what the product does to your machine and your data, and a framework is not that.

A framework is something a developer imports; it does not give you a running environment, a transcript you can read, or an approval gate. A harness does, and that is why the questions you ask a vendor differ: where does the transcript live, what may the tools touch, and who approves an action. If a product calls itself an "AI harness" and cannot answer those three, the label is decoration.

**Read next**

[What an agent harness does with your request](https://upahje.my/en/articles/using-the-harness)

[More on agent harnesses](https://upahje.my/en/articles/category/definitions)
